A GOOD story is going around. A gentleman re- ceived a visit from an acquaintance, who asked him if he would kindly lend him a certain work he was anxious to see, and which he felt pretty sure his friend had in his library. "Yes," said the gentleman in question, "I have it. But I am • sorry I can't lend it you. I make it a rule never to lend books." "But why?" said the visitor. "Because no one ever returns them," replied the other. "And to show you how true this is, I would ask you to cast your eye over the shelves before you. You see there my library, containing some 3,000 volumes. Well, they were all bor- rowed." WHEN a now famous politician who had just married a young wife was appointed to an import- ant Under-Secretaryship, his bride spent a week in house-hunting, and finally found what seemed to be a. suitable residence for an official of State. His first question was :—" What is the rent, dear?" " ill,ooo a year." The M.P. lapsed into deep thought, and the young wife said, rather nerv- ously :—" Do you think it extravagant ? " "It is not that," returned her husband, slowly. " I was wondering what I should do with the other £5OO of my salary." The hand upon his throat was loosened, and yet he only gasped in his great terror. "Captain Harold Travers, of that fiendish crew thou art the last! Host know me ?" " GLENALPINE !" "Thou hest said it! One more name thou may- eat speak. Address thyself to God if thou haat the courage to take that sacred name upon thy lips 1" • • • • Ali Arthur Rainsford—for while he wore his cap- tain's uniform he wore that oatoe—ii as aroused lrotn his painful reverie by a sound that startled him. It was not the quantity of the sound, but the quality that vibrated upon his sense. There was something in the faint notes that jarred upon the air with a ghostly thrill—something that crept to his inner-being with a touch of horror. He stopped and listened. The discordant dote was hushed, and he fancied that he now heard a voice raised in prayer. Presently he moved off again, and when he next looked up he beheld two men approaching him. One of them he was sure was Jasper Wallace. In a moment more they came to where the rays from one of the lanterns tell upon them, and he distinguished the general's features. The man with him was in uniform. Our hero was advancing for the purpose of saluting his friend, and Sir Jasper, who seemed to have recognized him in turn, was apparently hurrying Up for the same purpose, when a man stepped out from the hedge and stood between them. He had come within the rays of the lantern, and the tall, gaunt form and weird garb of the Wanderer was revealed. Arthur recog- nized him in a moment. He knew him for the man whom he had seen at the wayside inn in Yorkshire. But Sir Jasper was the first to speak. " Glenalpine !" "Aye, Wallace; we meet again. Did you come to seek me?" " No, Sir Phillip. I came to seek him who stands behind yoa." Glenalpine started as though a pistol had ex- ploded at his ear. He turned, and had taken a step towards our hero, when he saw the handsome, youthful face that shrank before him. He stopped and cast a huiried glance towards the hedge, and then shook off the momentary terror that had evi- dantly seized him. "I think I recognise the youth," he said. "Art thou not Arthur Berwick, otherwise called after thine own father, Arthur Rainsford?" "You are right," sir, answered Arthur, wonder- ingly. "And," added Sir Jasper, eagerly, at the same time stepping forward as though he would shield the young man from possible harm, "let me intro- duce him to you, Sir Phillip Glenalpine, as one of the noblest and truest friends I have in the world." Glenalpine nodded, but did not offer his hand. Once his hand seemed raised for that purpose, but he thrust it back out of sight. "Sir Jasper," he said, "you are my debtor." " I am not sorry for that.' "You owe me a life." "A life, Sir Philip?" "Aye, the life of your young friend." "Of Arthur 1 In Heaven's name, man what Is

It? Speak I" "Sir Jasper," pursued Glenalpine, in low, solemn cadence, "this night, and in this place, a villain sought to strike from his path a rival who stood between himself and the heirship of a peer- age. That rival he had long sought to crush and destroy, but his wicked wiles had not succeeded. At length he saw that fortune at every turn of her wheel was favouring the man he feared and hated. There wan Int oa_e recourse_ left, and of that he

talla avail liiineelf quickly, if at all. TO-night he came hither and laid himself in ambush, prepared for the work of assassination. But I had followed him. I hung upon him as Nemesis hung upon those whom she had marked for vengeance. Hi victim was approaching, all unconscious of the impending evil, and he was prepared to strike when I laid my hand upon him. Ile knew me—he called my name 1" " Was Arthur the intended victim? " asked Sir Jasper, shuddering with horror.
"Yes." _ "And the would-be assassin—"

"Come hither," said Glenalpine. He took Sir Jasper by the arm and led him to a spot directly beneath the neighbouring lantern, and there, where the light was strong, he drew the leather bag from his bosom and took out the blood-red book. He opened it and pointed to a page whereon a name was written, and he asked Sir Jasper if he could read it. The old soldier held the book nearer to the light, and read and pro. pounced the name aloud: "HAROLD :TRAVERS !"

dkbaid they bore me away; and gavii dut at linckltoeat that I was dead. I was smuggled back to the regiment, and as we were ordereu to Ports- mouth on the very next day, the cheat was not discovered at the manor. Little did I think what a scheme of villainy I was helping, and much less did I think that I was to bring misery and wretch- edness upon my sweet sister. But look up Mary. Say that you forgive me." She reL.ched up and kissed him. Sha tried to speak, but her utterance was broken into hysterical sobs.
"My pet you will forgive me ?" "0, yes, yes, Lionel! But there is another." She was hanging upon his neck, with her face buried in her bosom.

Then Glenalpine took from his pocket a small silver box in which was a black pigment, of the consistence of paste, and he dipped his finger therein, and with it drew a broad, heavy line up and down the page, cutting the name in two equal halves. Then he dipped his finger again, and drew another line across the page, from left to right. And thus a Black Cross was made, and the arms thereof had overshadowed and for ever' obliterated the name that had neen written upon the page. "Sir Jasper," said the worn and weary man, when he had put up the book, "my work is done; Glenalpine's Oath is fulfilled !" Wallace caught him by the arm, and pointed towards the hedge. Glenalpine understood the sign, and answered: He is there. It was as I told you. He had come out to lie in wait for his step-brother, and was ready to deal the fatal blow, when my wait- ing hand fell upon him. Sir Jasper, though the deed was in my heart from the time long agone, yet I am glad that it was permitted me to strike this life in the saving of another and a better.— No, no,—go not thither. Look not upon the work my hands have done. Know that the wretch is dead, and that your friend is saved. I will call proper officers, and on the morrow I shall surren- der myself to the Governor General." "Right, right, Sir Philip. I will be with you. Fear not to trust his lordship." "Did I hear aright?" asked Arthur, when Sir Jasper returned. "Did I hear the name of Harold spoken?" "Yes, my boy." "And was it he who sought my life?" "Aye, it was your step-brother, Harold." "Harold Berwick !" cried the officer who had accompanied Sir Jasper' and who had been stand- ing in the back ground. "Merciful heavens! to what a base and black-hearted villain did I sell myself. Arthur! my dear boy !—" Hush ! " interposed Sir Jasper, entreatingly. "Draw not observation to this place. Let us retire, and we can talk as we walk on. Or—stop, —I have it. Do you two go on together, and tell your stories as you ge. I will post of and find Lord Bit climear. lie must be with us to-night. If you reach the house before us, wait for us in the garden." • At a later hour some officers, guided by Glen- alpine, came to the spot, and from beyond the hedge they dragged a heavy burden, which they lifted in their ararS and bore away towards the citadeL
CHAPTER. XVIII. CONCLUSION.

It was I,,te in the evening when Elsie Nolan, coming in from the garden, entered the drawing- room. Her footfall in the hall had aroused Mary Wallace, who had been slumbering upon a sofa. Poor girl ! She was worn and weary, and her lids had been heavy. She had been waiting for her guardian. but he did not come. She had started to her feet, and was gazing eagerly around when her maid entered. _ . _
He lifted her gently up and kissed her upon the bi ovv.

"My dear mistress !" cried Elsie, started for- ward, "your eye is bright, and there has been a smile upo i your face. 0 ! has good come ?" " Alas ! dear Elsie, it was but a dream." "And dreams are not always empty. Who knows—"
" Hush ! Such bright dreams must evermore be vain for me !" Mary resumed her seat upon the sofa, and then added:
"Elsie, have you been out ?"

"Yea, lady." - "Have you heard anything? Can you tell me of —of ?" "They say he has made application to be sent to his regiment at Agra." Mary pressed her folded hands upon her bosom, and a rno4n of pain escaped her lips. "It is better so," she said, after a time. "Better !" cried Elsie, in a shocked tone. Rernemoer, she had lost no brother. She only remembered that Captain Arthur was the bravest and handsomest and most pleasant-spoken gentle- man s'ros had ever known. "Do you not know that all the troops at Agra are to be sent away into that dreauful Puoja.ub ? He will be killed there, lady." He vill die a soldier's death— he will die bravely. Elsie." " And you—you—my dear mistress ?" "I shall not long survive him, my child." "0 1 it is wicked, wicked, wicked, for you to talk like that." "Hark 1 There is some one in the hall, Elsie. Go and see if it is your master." Elsie opened the door, and met Sir Jasper in the entrance. He came in, and went up and took Mary's hand. My dear girl. I have been out. 1 have heard news. Are you strong enough to listen ?" "I know all, Sir Jasper. Ile is going to join his regiment." "And you will see him before he goes?" "No !—No! I dare not." "Not even to speak one last word of good will ?" "0! my guardian, you do not know what you would have me do. Would you bid the outcast pen i return to gaze upon the heaven from which she has been banished forever ?" _ _
"But—my dear girl— Bless me I what shall I lay!" "Guardian I What is it? There is a new light in your eye. 0! is there hope? Can there be— Alas ! the one dread blow hath fallen !"

"Who says a blow hath fallen? Zounds ! my girl, you must be strong. Suppose the very heaven itself should open at this minute, and all its daz- zling glory shine down upon you. Would you be able to bear it ?"

" Guardian! Sir Jasper 1" She caught his hands and gazed eagerly up into his face. What meant the marvellous light that struggled in his eyes, gleaming through gathering tears, and giving a radiance like noonday to his countenance? Why did he try to hide the smile which sprang again and again to the surface in spite of him? Why did •. he tremble and turn his gaze so nervously towards the door ! Vho was it ? What was it? " 0 1 guardian ! in God's name, tell me if there is a break in the dark and bitter night I" " You ate strong enough to see an angel, Mary ?" He did not wait for an answer. He put her from him gently, and turned to the door. There was a movement of feet—a few whispered words—a hush—and the wondering girl ventured to look up. And she saw standing before her, with the rays of the astral lamps shining full upon his face, her own dear brother whom she had thought dead. She turned one quick glance upon her guardian— she saw the radiance of his face taking to itself celestial lustre—and she knew that it was no dream.
"Mary !" "'Lionel Lionel! My brother I Not dead ! 0! not dead !"

And she flew to his outstretched arms, and clung to him as clings the dying upon a new life. "My poor sister !" whispered Lionel, kissing her again, and then lifting her head so that he could look into her face. "And they told you I was dead ?"

"HE has forgiven me, Mary, and at heart we are true and loving brothers. Ask him and he will tell you.,, No need to tell her more—no need to tell her that another had come to make deeper and brighter her joy—no need to make her look up. She heard the step—she felt the thrill of the great love vibrating till her heart was lost in holy rapture—and she 'knew that Arthur's strong arms entwined her, and that upon the bosom of her dear lover she was rest- ing in peace and in safety, No need that her guardian should bless the Teunion—no need that Lord Birchmear should lay (his hands upon their heads, and weep in his new- found joy—no need that Lionel should swear that lit was the happiest moment of his life; no need of All this—for, looking up into Arthur's face once more, and catching the light supernal of those true and loving eyes, sbe knew, as with prophetic faith, that nothing in life could shatter the cup which had thus been pressed, brimming with blessings to her lips ! • • •

" Yes." "And they made you believe that Arthur had killed me ?" "Yea! 0! yes!" " 0 ! my darling My poor, dear pet, what a villain I made of myself !" He still held her in his arms as he told the story. "It was a base and wicked plot from first to last; but, as God is my judge, I knew not the full extent of the harm that was meant. I dreamed not that Harold Berwick sought real injury to his step-brother. He told me it was only a lark. He said Arthur was a boaster, and he wished to give him a lesson, and I entered into his plot. 01 all wrong on that occa- kion Arthur is as innocent as the babe unborn. We plied him with liquor, and I cheated him pur- posely. I led him on to the blow he gave me. And yet it was not I. Harold was the leading spirit. There were no bullets in the pistols we used. And yet Arthur would not fire upon me rntil they foro_e_hita. I fell, as I had nronaised

Our story would hardly be complete without a few more words, by way of addenda., touching some of our principal characters. " Sir Philip Gleualpine went to the Governor- General, as lie had promised, and told the story of his sad and eventful life. Sir Jasper was present, hut his friendly offices were not needed. Sir Philip was at liberty. But Sir Philip cared not to return to England; and he could net live a life of idleness, which would leave him only to reflec- tion upon the past; and the Governor-General, at the request of Lord Birchmear, installed him into an important and responsible office at Patna. Lady Birchmear, when she knew what the fates had done, was utterly crushed and broken. All her wickedness was known, and she could not face those whom she would have so deeply wronged. She had no desire to return to England. She selected a retired dwelling in Calcutta, which her husband gave to her use, and he also made arrange- ments for the payment of an annuity sufficient fur her utmost wants.

A few years passed away, and Lionel Talford, grown into a new and better manhood since his experience at the hands of Harold Berwick, had. risen to the rank of colonel. One day, as he sat in his quarters at Lucknow, a courier arrived with the mail, and among the letters from England was one for himself. He opened it, and found it to be from his uncle ; and as he read, a warm, ruddy glow broke through the dark sun-tan of his face. "My dear boy," wrote Sir Jasper, "I am sorry to deprive the service of so good an officer as I am proud to know you are universally acknowledged; bu . you are wanted in England. Arthur and Mary have put their heads together in open rebellion, and declare that my estate in Devonshire may go to the crown before they will allow it as my ward's dowry; and they even hint that if I do not make you master of Oakside, they will never visit the grand old place again. But, bless your soul! they know how my heart has leaned since I knew how much good there was in you. So come, Lionel— my son—and accept the honourable position which awaits you. Should you find Oakside ever dull, I will take you to Birchmear, where the glorious sunshine is continuous. There Sir John and I can fight our battles o'er again, while you and Arthur and Mary—But come, and you shall see for your- self. You will find all necessary arrangements for your transfer ready made at the Government House in Calcutta."

To this Sir Jasper's hardy sign-manual was af- fixed. And then, in a delicate, fairly-like hand, a postscript was written, signed by Arthur and Mary Berwicsk ; and Lionel read, through thick-coming tears: 4. COMP. LiortAl.—onmA. ,nr hrother,—and make &ueeue La our surpas:n .g joy."

The " Sun "makes an announcement which will be read with great interest in certain circles. It is to the effect that Miss Vanderbilt, a great American heiress, is to receive the sum of two millions sterling rrom her family when she marries the Duke of Marlborough. and that the Duke himself will " not be forgotten." " His Grace "is to receive no less than £600,000, "soas to enable him entirely to free his estate of any encum- brances."

CHAPTER I. THE NOCTURNAL VISIT. * ** Whence is that knocking? How is't with me when every sound appals me? * * * I hear a knocking In the south entry I Hark !—more knocking! SHAKESPEARE. Hurricane Hall is a large old family mansion, built of dark, red sandstone, in one of the loneliest, and wildest of the mountain regions of Virginia. The estate is surrounded on three sides by a range of steep, grey rocks, spiked with clumps of dark evergreens, and called, from its horseshoe form, the Devil's Hoof. On the fourth side the ground gradually descends In broken rock and barren soil to the edge of the wild mountain stream known as the Devil's Run. When storms and floods were high, the loud roar- ing of the wild mountain gorges, and the terrific raging of the torrent over its rocky course, gave to this savage locality its ill-omened names of Devil's Hoof, Devil's Run, and Hurricane Hall. Major Ira Warfield, the lonely proprietor of the Hall, was a veteran officer, who, in disgust at what he supposed to be ill-requited services, had retired from public life to spend the evening of his vigorous age on this his patrimonial estate. Here he lived in seclusion, with his old-fashioned housekeeper, Mrs. Condiment, and his old family servants and his favourite dogs and horses. Here his mornings were usually spent in the chase, in which he ex- celled, and his afternoons and evenings were occu- pied in small convivial suppers among his few chosen companions of the cthase or the bottle. In person Major Warfield was tall and strongly built, reminding one of some old iron-limbed Douglas of the olden time. His features were large and harsh; his complexion dark red, as that of one bronzed by long exposure and flushed with strong drink. His fierce, dark grey eyes were surmounted by thick, heavy black brows, that, when gathered into a frown, reminded one of a thunder-cloud, as the flashing orbs beneath them did of lightning. His hard, harsh face was surrounded by a thick growth of iron-grey hair and beard that met be- neath his chin. His usual habit was a black cloth coat, crimson vest, black leather breeches, long, black yarn 'stockings, fastened at the knees, and morocco slippers with silver buttons. In character Major Warfield was arrogant, domi- neering and violent—equally loved and feared by his faithful old family servants at home—disliked an dreaded by his neighbours and acquaintances abroad, who, partly from his house and partly from his character, fixed upon him the appropriate Nick- name of OLD HURRICANE. There was, however, other ground of dislike be- sides that of his arrogant mind, violent temper and domineering habits. Old Hurricane was said to be an old bachelor, yet rumour whispered that there was in some obscure part of the world, hidden away from human sight, a deserted wife and child, poor, forlorn, and heartbroken. It was farther whis- pered that the elder brother of Ira Warfield had mys- teriously disappeared, and not without some suspicion of foul play on the part of the only person in the world who had a strong interest in his "taking off." However these things might be, it was known for a certainty that Old Hurricane had an only sister, widowed, sick, and poor, who with her son dragged on a wretched life of ill-requited toil, severe privation, and painful infirmity, in a dis- tant city, unaided, unsought, and uncared for by her _

It was the night of the last day of October, eighteen hundred and forty-five. The evening had closed in dark and gloomy. Alput dusk the wind arose in the north-west, driving up masF es 01 leaden- hued clouds, and in a few minutes the ground was covered deep with snow, and the air was filled with driving sleet. As this was All Hallow Eve, the dreadful in- clemency of the weather did not prevent the negroes of Hurricane Hall from availing themselves of their capricious old master's permission, and going off in body to a banjo break-down, held in the negro quarters of their next neighbour. Upon this evening, then, there was left at Hurri- cane Hall only Major Warfield ; Mrs. Condiment, his little old housekeeper; and Wool, his body- servant.

Early in the evening the old hall was shut up closely to keep out as much as possible the sound of the storm that roared through the mountain chasms, and cannonaded the walls of the house as if determined to force an entrance. As soon as she had seen that all was safe, Mrs. Condiment went to bed and went to It was about ten o'clock that night that Old Hurricane, well wrapped up in his quilted flannel dressing-gown, sat in his well-padded easy chair before a warm and bright fire, taking his comfort in his own most comfortable bed-room. This was the hour of the cosiest enjoyment to the self-indulgent old Sybarite, who dearly loved his own ease. And Indeed every means and appliance of bodily comfort was at hand. Strong oaken shutters and thick heavylcurtains at the windows kept out every draught of air, and so deadened the sound of the wind that its subdued moaning was just sufficient to remind one of the stormy weather without in contrast to the bright warmth within. Old Hurricane, as I said, sat well wrapped up in his wadded dressing- gown, and reclining in his padded easy chair, with his head thrown back and his feet upon the fire- irons, toasting his shins and sipping his punch. On his right hand stood a little table with a lighted candle, a stack of clay pipes, a jug of punch, lemons, sugar, Holland gin, Ste., while on the hearth sat a kettle of boiling water to help to replenish the jag If needful. On his left band stood his cosy bedstead with its warm crimson curtains festooned back,, revealing the luxurious swell of the full feather bed, and pillows with their snow white linen, and lambswool blankets inviting repose. Between this bedstead and the corner of the fire-place stood Old Hurri- cane's ancient body servant, Wool, engaged in warning a crimson cloth nightcap. "'Sdeath, sir I do you think that I am going to turn a deaf ear to a stranger that comes to my house for shelter on such a night as this? Go and answer the bell directly." "Yes, sar." "But stop—look here, sirrah—mind, I am not to be disturbed. If it is a, traveller, ask him in, set refreshments before him, and show him to bed. I'm not going to leave my warm room to welcome anybody to•night, please the L•:.•rd. Do you hear?" "Yes, sar," said the darkey, retreating. As Wool took a shaded taper and opened the door leading from his master's chamber, the wind was heard howling through the long passages ready to burst into the cosy bedroom. "SHUT THE DOOR, you scoundrel!" roared the old man, folding the skirt of his warm dressing- gown across his knees, and hovering closer to the fire. Wool quickly obeyed, and was heard retreating down the steps. "Whew!" said the old man, spreading his hands over the blaze with a look of comfortable apprecia- tion. "What would induce me to go abroad on such a night as this? Wind blowing great guns from the north-west—snow falling fast from the heavens, and rising just as fast before the wind from the ground I—cold as Lapland, dark as Erebus I No telling the earth from the sky. Whew!" and to comfort the cold thought, Old Hurricane poured out another glass of smoking punch, and. began to sip It. • "Hew I thank the Lord that lam not a doctor! If I were a doctor now, the sound of that bell at this kour of night would frighten me; I should think some old woman had been taken with the pleurisy, and wanted me to get up and go out in the storm, to turn out of my warm bed to ride ten miles through the snow to prescribe for her. A doctor never can feel sure, even in the worst of weathers, of a good night's rest. But, thank heaven, I am free from all such annoyances, and if I am sure of anything in this world it is of my comfortable night's sleep," said Old Hurricane, as he sipped his punch, smacked his lips and toasted his feet. At this moment Wool re-appeared. "SHUT THE DOOR, you villain! Do you intend to stand there holding it open on me all night 2" vociferated the old man. Wool hastily closed the offending portals, and hurried to his master's side. "Well, sir, who was it rung the bell?" "Please, Marster, sir, it wer de Reverend Mr. Parson Goodwin." " Goodwin ? Been to make a sick-call, I suppose, and got caught in the snow-storm. I declare it is as bad to be a parson as it is to be a doctor. Thank the Lord lam not a parsoh either; if I were now, I might be called away from my cosy arm-chair and fire-side to ride twelve miles to comfort some old man dying of quinsy. Wool, here—help me into bed, pile on more comforters, tuck me up warm, put a bottle of hot water to my feet, and then go and attend to the parson," said the old man, getting up and moving towards his inviting couch. " Sar 1 ear! stop, sar, if you please!" cried Wool, going after him. • "Why, what does the old fool mean," exclaimed Old Hurricane, angrily. " Sar, de Reverend Mr. Parson Goodwin say how he must see you yourse'f, personable, alone!" • "See me, you villain! Didn't you tell him that I had retired?" "Yes, Marse, f tell him how you wer' gone to bed and asleep more'n an hour ago, and he ordered me to come wake you up, and say how it were a matter o' life and deaths" "Life and death? What have I to do with life

and death 9 I won't stir ! If the parson wants to see me, he will have to come up here and see me in bed," exclaimed Old Hurricane, suiting the action to the word, by jumping into bed and drawing all the comforters and blankets up around his head and shoulders. " Mus' I fetch his reverence up, sar 9" "Yes, I wouldn't get up and go down to see— Washington—SHUT THE DOOR, you rascal, or I'll throw the bootjack at your wooden head 1" Wool obeyed with alacrity, and in time to es- cape the threatened missile. After an absence of a few minutes he was heard returning, attending upon the footsteps of another. And the next minute he entered, ushering in the Rev. Mr. Goodwin, the parish minister of Bethlehem, Sc. Mary's.

"How do you do? How do you do? Glad to see you, sir I glad to see you, though obliged to re- ceive you in bed 1 Fact is, I caught a cold with this severe change of weather, and took a warm negus and went to bed to sweat it off 1 You'll excuse me! Wool, draw that easy chair up to my bedside for worthy Mr. Goodwin, and bring him a glass of warm negus! It will do him good after his cold ride!" "I thank you, Major Warfield 1 I will take the seat, but not the negus, if you please, to-night." "Not the negus 1 Oh, come now, you are joking Why, it will keep you from catching cold, and be a most comfortable night-cap, disposing you to sleep and sweat like a baby Of course you spend the night with us?" " I thaak you, no. I must take the road again in a few minutes." "Take the road again to night! Why, man alive, It is midnight, and the snow driving like all Lap- land I" "Sir, I am sorry to refuse your proffered hospitality, and leave your comfortable roof to- night, and sorrier still to have to take you with me," said the pastor, gravely. "Take ME with you! No, no, my good sir—no, no, that is too good a joke—ha! ha!" "Sir, I fear that you will find it a very serious one I—Your servant told you that my errand was one of imminent urgency?" " Yes, something like life and death—" "Exactly—down in the cabin near the Punch Bowl, there is an old woman dying--" "There—l knew it! I was just saying there might be an old woman dying! But, my dear sir, what's that to me? What can Ido ? " "Humanity, sir, would prompt you!" "But, my dear sir, how can I help her I am not a physician to prescribe—" "She is far past a physician's help 1" " Nor am I a priest to bear her confession—* "Her confession God has already perceived." "Well, and I'm not a lawyer to draw up her will!" "No, sir; but you are recently appointed one of the Justices of the Peace of Allegheny ? " "Yes I well, what of that? That does not comprise the duty of getting up out of my warm bed and going through a snow-storm to see an old woman expire." "I regret to inconvenience you, sir • but in this Instance you duty demands your attendance at the _

Let's have a short talk with short words. As for my- self, I always did like people to talk so that I could un• derstand them the first time, and not have to over- haul their words afterwards to find out what they want to say. Did you ever see people who made you think of a rabbit in the grass, always looking out for things to get scared at and to run away from ? Of course. Now what is natural in a rabbit may not be so in a man. The rabbit can't fight, and so he has to run. But a human being ought not to get flustered so easily. We are made to stand our ground better. Yet grown men sometimes seem to be as fidgety and full of alarms as deenceless little animals.

Here is one who says, " If any one knocked at the door it set my heart all in a flutter." We won't say that this man wanted common courage, for that isn't true. He was naturally as plucky as you are, but something had gone wrong with him. Poke a straw against the back of a man's hand and he takes no notice ; poke it n his eye and he does. Now every sound that comes to the ear strikes against a set of nerves—little white cords—inside of it, and the nerves carry the news to the brain, close by. When these nerves are in good form we don't mind one sound in ten thousand. But when they are sore, weak, and tender, a penny dropped on the floor makes a racket like the firing of a pistol. The person with the sore nerves jumps, and his heart struggles as a canary bird does when you hit its cage a whack with a stick—a mean thing to do. So you see a man may have courage enough to be a general in the army and still be upset by a sudden knock on his door. It is not the man, it is his nervous system that flutters. "No difference," you say? Yes there is—a lot of difference.

There. Now we will have the whole story in Mr. Shaw's own words, which are Bhort and plain as the words in the books our little ones read at school. He goes on to say," I am a boot and shoe maker, and have lived in the district 50 years. I was always sound and all right up to October, 1888. Then I fell ill without knowing what ailed me. My mouth tasted badly, my appetite failed, and after eating I had pain in the chest and sides. I often felt faint and dizzy, as if I should fail, and had a deal of paipitation of the heart. I got so nervous that if any one knocked at the door it set my heart all in a flutter. Later on I was seized with pains in the back and kidneys, that were like being stabbed with a knife. The secretion from my kidneys was thick and white and passed only with straining and difficulty. The pain in my bladder made me suffer like a martyr at the stake ; I was in agony with it day and night. My friends told me I had Bright's disease, and could not get well. I got so weak I could hardly walk, and often I could only work at my trade five minutes or so at a time.

"I took all kinds of medicine, bnt got no relief. In this way I lived along for three years, when a gentle- man living at Gainsboro' told me of Mother Seigel's Syrup. I bought a bottle at Broomhead's drug store, West Stockwith, and when I used it up I had no more pain, and the flow from my kidneys was of a natural colour. When I finished a second bottle I felt like a new man. By an occasional dose since then I keep in good health. My friends say that my recovery is a mira- cle. After what I have gone through I am surprised to find myself alive and well. Several people who had the same complaint, and had the best medical treatment are now in their graves. lam confident Seigel's Syrup would have cured them. (Signed), William Shaw, East Stockwith, near Gainsboro', January 3rd, 1893." We end this plain and impressive case in a few more short words. Mr. Shaw's complaint was indigestion and dyspepsia, which both starved and poisoned his nerves, and would, no doubt, soon have wholly stopped the beating of that troubled heart of his. Thank Mer- cy he got the remedy before it was too late : Minds and bodies, bodies and minds I Yet where is our cour- age, power, and skill when these poor bodies are torn by disease P To help us at such times is the mission of good Mother Seigel.

Nevada (U.S.A.) has a bed of salt covering an area of 15,930 acreas. Its bottom has never been discovered. If there were but one potato in the world, a careful cultivator might produce 10,000,000,000 from it in ten years, and that would supply the world with seed once more. _ _ .
A law in Basle, Switzerland, prohibits the occupancy of a house until tour weeks after it has been completed. This is to prevent disease from damp walls.

Dr. Bertillon has discovered a new method identifying handwriting, The letters are enlarged by means of photography, and irregularities,due to the beating of the pulse, and then measured. By comparison a valuable clue is obtained. _ .

There is something beautifully expressive and homely in the abbreviation of father, "Dad," yet probably very few sons and daughters know that in using that word they are speaking the purest Welsh. The opening words of the Lord's Prayer, in Welsh, are "Emn Dad." Mare's milk is in Use among the Tartars, as it was in the days of Herodotus among the Scythians,and as asses' rnik is in Abyssinia. The ass and the mule have been in some countries the royal animals on which only kings and princes were allowed to ride. Marriages by proxy are contracted to this day in Hol- land, and are mostly put in practice by Dutchmen who, having gone abroad, prefer to marry the girls they left behind them, in this convenient manner, than go to the expense and probable inconvenience of returning to Hol- land for the purpose of the ordinary marriage solemniza- tion. After the legal preliminaries are executed,a friend marries the bride by proxy, and she is thereafter promptly shipped off to her new home. A revolting state of matters prevails in connection with rice cultivation in Mazanderan and Ghilan,south of the Caspian Sea. In the spring a landowner marries as many wives as he needs to cultivate his fields. When the autumn harvesting is done these wives are divorced, to avoid the expense of supporting them over winter. Polygamy in its worst form is the custom throughout the province. " We met," says Dr. Wishard, " one man not a rico-planter, but a merchant, sixty-three years of age, who first married at the age of eighteen. He had now four wives, and during his eighteen years of married life had had and divorced twenty other wives.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAREST NELLIE, I hear on good authority that everything will be Oriental this winter, in the way of trimmings; the new silks are truly gorgeous in old Cashmere pat- terns, the multitude of colours so deftly inwoven that the effect is a richly-tinted, harmonious whole. without one garish tone about it. In the spring a good many pine pattern silks and crêpes were shown, but these look large and crude beside the autumn designs. The autumn fashions in walking costumes pre- sent, so far, very little novelty. The most im- portant change is in the make of the sleeves. These will be worn without any stiffening, and in shape somewhat resembling the so-called leg-of- mutton sleeve, of which I think I have already told you. Bodices to match the skirts will be the order of the day, trimmed with Louis XV. and Louis XVI. embroideries. The leading houses are making very pretty woollen dresses with plain skirts, a trifle less voluminous than those worn of late, and bodices with basques, edged with fiat or rolled silken embroideries. I have specially ad- mired a Louis XV. trimming of pale-green silk, covered a net-work of black silk, and tiny coloured embossed flowers at regular intervals, upon a blue- grey woollen gown, ornamenting the wide square revers, the collar, the centre of the back, and the slightly undulating basque. The back fits tightly without seems; a full narrow silk vest is intro- duced in the front of the bodice.

As to cloaks, sealskin, as I told you last week, is what nearly everyone will wear this winter. Here, for instance, is a rather large sealskin cape. so full that it falls in positive folds. The collar is

sable, and the epaulettes are edged with sable, and start from under very smart seal rosettes. The manipulation of rosettes from a fur is decidedly curious, and by no means easy. Hats this autumn are to be smaller than those we have worn during the summer. Some very pretty shapes and trimmings hail from Paris, and I must try and give you some idea of the new capotes and round hats, as they are termed. The capotes are lovely. One is a beguin in coloured stones, with merely a black aigrette and a" bunch of roses resting on the hair in front, a little on one side, but it has the real Parisian cachet. The other is in seal, with long ears, a la Charlotte Corday, caught with strass ornaments; the front is slightly raised with violets and gardenias, that have a charming effect upon the dark fur. A petty hat is the -Homburg, which is rather a large one. It has fan bows or rich black satin rain-

proof ribbon, and boasts a lovely paste buckle and erect speckled wings. This is a most becoming chapeau. Eton and bolero fronts are still worn, and a useful kind of gown of rather dark green cloth has its bodice cut with short rounded, fronts, edged with a narrow line of brown fur. The tight-fitting vest is of tan cloth, striped with close-set horizontal lines of dark green braid and the bodice is finished at the waist by a rather wide-folded sash of still deeper green silk. Another pretty fur-trimmed frock has for material a brown knotted tweed. The skirt has narrow lines of brown fur running down the side seams, and the rounded yoke of drab cloth is similariy edged, the fronts of the bodice below the latter being arranged in three box pleats, with narrow bands of the drab cloth between them, while the full basque is lined with drab satin. For immediate wear a useful gown.is of 'rather bright navy-blue serge; the skirt is plain and unstiffened, and the upper part of the front of bodice is pleated fully, and slightly overhangn a„ sort of sash of red and cream striped soft silk cut, on the cross, which, starting from the under-arm, seams, is drawn to the front, and, tied in a kneC with ends of considerable length. The back of' the bodice reaches just a. shade below the waist, but has no basque, and the sleeves are of the bishop shape, cut with long shoulder-seams, and finished with small undercuffs of the striped silk.
Jackets show very little change this year, except that there is a tendency for the sleeves to get smaller. One I liked very much had moderate-

sized revers edged with broad braid, and there are braid trimmings on each side of the jacket and extending upwards from the cuffs. Altogether a very stylish jacket. Woollen dresses that have been put aside during the summer may be successfully washed, if care is taken and soft water used. 'Grease spots should be first removed with benzine. Let the dress lie in some good soapy washing water, and the dirt will then, in a measure' come out without rubbing. The water must not be too hot, and no soda must be used. Two rinsing. waters will be required, the first warm, the last cold. Hang in the air to dry, without wringing, and iron while slightly damp. Your loving, Jrartint.

div.head: New Way to Make Money.
div.p: A New Way to Make Money.

A clever Pittsburg girl, barely twenty -years of age, has started a new business, and is earning a substantial income for herself by making aprons. Left an orphan when only thirteen years old, she undertook the work as a means of support. At first she canvassed from house to house ; but now she needs but to take orders, as her work is known to be satisf ictory. As aprons are a necessity of the wardrobe and in constant wear and tear, a market which brings the same to the door has csme to be greatly appreciated both by mistress and maid, and she has her regular round of patrons. She menu- factures her aprons through the winter and spring, and usually devotes about six weeks in the summer to the taking of orders and the delivery of the goods. She is mostsystematic in her method of work. Some days are spent in running up nothing but ties or strings, yard after yard being run off and divided into proper lengths. Other days are devoted to nothing but the hemming of the bottoms of the aprons, whilst, again, other days there is nothing done bet gathering. All work is done on the machine, and at present sbe has no assistants. No fancy aprons are manufactured, none with bibs, and none for children. The largest business is done in the nursemaid aprons,these of double breadth,full almost to dress-skirt pattern. Thi; sewing aprons have d:_ep pockets, and in a few of the dainty lawn aprons for the mistress there is a jaunty pocket. She confesses that on an apron which sells for fifty cents., the actual out- lay, owing to her wholesale purchase of material, is but a trifle over sixteen cents. Last year her income came to something over six hundred pounds.
The Six Richest Women.

Who are the six richest women in the world ? They are Senora Cousino, Miss Hetty Green, the Baroness Burdett-Coutts, Mme. de Barrios (or, more properly speaking, the Marquise de Rods), Miss Mary Garrett, of Baltimore, and Mme. Woleska, the great Russian land- owner. Senora Cousin° is a South American widow reputed to be worth forty millions sterling. This lady owns vast expanses of land, many cattle-ranges, a fleet of eight steamships, silver, copper, and coal mines, rail- roads, and many houses,besides personal property in the form of splendid jewels. She is probably the richest woman in the world. Just how much all her wealth amounts to no one knows, probably not even Senora Cousin° herself. From her coal mines alone, it is stated, her income is seventeen thousand pounds a month. From her silver and copper mines she receives the larger sum of twenty thousand pounds net, and uses the refuse from the coal mine to smelt the ore from the mines of silver and copper. Then her stock farms, whereon she breeds thoroughbred horses and:cattle, and her ranches, yield about as much as all her mining property put together. Miss Betty Green is supposed to be worth ten million pounds, and to be the richest woman in North America. The Marquise de Rods is the wife of a Span- ish grandee. She is a Guatemalan by birth, and Be Barrios, then President of the Republic,married her from a convent at the age of fourteen, disposing of the objec- tions of the Mother Superior by locking that lady up. The tyrannous Dictator made a fortune out of his pre- sidentship, and when :he was shot dead by a patriot lying in ambush in the suburbs of the capital his widow found herself worth five million pounds. Miss Mary Garrett, of Baltimore, is worth two million pounds, which is in stock of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad. Mme. Woleska is credited with wealth to the same amount. All these ladies are, it is said, quite capable of managing their affairs, and equal to the wiles of the cleveresz, sharper.
Remember this if You're Asked.

The fond parents who are presented with a newly-born infant on February 29th next will be in a rather awk- ward position ; they will be unable to make the first birthday party for eight years to come. For, as most people have been informed, there is no leap-year be- tween 1896 and 1904. In a little while everybody will be asking the reason of this arbitrary conduct on the part of the calendar makers, and will want to know the " why and the wherefore "of the rule that " the cen- tury years are to be counted ordinary years and not leap-years." As a matter of fact the statement is not strictly correct, for the year 2000 will be having a 29th of February. The whole secret of the confusion lies in the inconsiderate action on the part ot the earth, which in ite year of revolution round the sun, rotates an odd fraction—ninety-seven four-hundreths—in addition to its 365 times. Bow to dispose of the fraction was the problem which puzzled Pope Gregory in the sixteenth cen ury,just as it had puzzled the Romans of old. The Romans got out of the difficulty, however, in a very simple fashion, by counting the fraction of a day as a quarter,and waited till they could add the four quarters as an extra day at the end of their year, which com- menced with March. This means 100 days added in the space of four centuries ; but to get the exact 97, Pope Gregory ordained that the century years themselves should not be counted (thus omitting four of them), but as an extra day was then wanted to make the 97, it should be counted in at the 400th year, that is the one that can be exactly divided by the number 400. Thus, while the years 2100, 2200, 2300, will not he leap years, the years 2000 and 2400. Cassell's Saturday Journal."

div.head: Specks Before the Eves.
div.p: Specks Before the Eves.

Specks before the eyes, or Muscre Volitantes, are says the" Family Physician," of common occurrence in con- nection with megrim, or sick headache. They often occur, however, without any accompanying headache. Their great characteristic is their incessant movement, for by no effort of the will can they be kept quiet even i for a moment. They come into the field of vision,traverse it, and then suddenly disappear. Sometimes they are I black, and at others quite bright, like little specks of light. They are seen quite as distinctly when the eyes are closed aa when they are open. They may occur at any age,bat are mast common in those who have passed the meridian of life, and often enough they are associ- ated with short-sightedness. Sometimes they depend on an abnormal perception of particles of dust floating in the fluid which moistens the eye, at others they are due to little particles floating about in the interior of the eye itself. They are usually most troublesome when the eyes have been tried over any fine work, especially if performed by candle-light, and they are intensified by worry and anxiety, or by anything which overtasks the brain or lowers the health. They do no harm, and as a rule cause no inconvenience. They may last for years, and then, perhaps from some change in occupation or mode of life, take their departure. If they are persist- ent and cause much uneasiness, it would be as well to have the eyes examined by an ophthalmic surgeon, to see if they are sound. Should no fault be detected, the patient cannot do better than live quietly and steadily, keep in as good health as possible, and ignore them. They should not be looked for. Plain glasses of neutral tint or dark cobalt-blue way render them less apparent. When there is antemia, iron will often effect a cure. In other cases belladonna may prove useful. Sometimes we meet with specks before the eves which, instead of being in constant movement,are quite stationary. These are of more serious import, and may be the precursor of cataract or other organic disease of the eye. They I are often associated with impairment of vision. In these cases an ophthalmic surgeon should be consulted. —From the" Family Physician " for March.

Mr. Alderman Duckworth has presented his new com- modious temperance hotel to the Rochdale Liberals as a club. Should the club be broken up at any time, the buildings are to be sold and the proceeds given to the Rochdale Infirmary. The hotel has been built and fitted up at a cost of £12,000.

div.head: NEW CH11742F CONSTABLE
div.p: THE NEW CH11742F CONSTABLE
OF WARRINGTON.

A joint meeting of the Watch and General Purposes Committees of the Warrington Town Council was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday last, for the purpose of choosing a successor to Mr. S.Hunt,the chief constable. It will be remembered that in response to the advertisement there were 30 applications for the post. At a meeting of the I two committees held on Monday week, this num- ber was reduced to seven, namely, InslActor David Hill,Bolton ; Superintendent D. Macintosh, Wigan; Inspector Pearson, Stockport ; Chief Detective In- spector Quigley, Stockport ; Mr. Luke Talbot,chief constable of Kendal ; Mr. George Taylor, chief con• stable of Newcastle-under-Lyne ; and Mr. A. W. Armour, chief constable of Windsor. All these with I the exception of the latter who was unable to be I present owing to illness, were at the Town Hall on Thursday afternoon. After about an hour's deliber- ation, during which the various candidates were interviewed,the Committees decided to appoint Mr. Luke Talbot to the post. The choice lay practi- cally between Mr. Talbot and Mr. Taylor. Mr. Tal- bot was, however, finally chosen unanimously. He will enter upon his duties at Warrington a month dating from his appointment. The choice has given great satisfaction among the public gener- ally, several members of the force being acquainted with him.

The following interesting account of the new Chief Constable is taken from " The Police Review and Parade Gossip," of January 4th :—Mr. Luke Talbot, Chief Constable of Kendal, was born in Bradford, Yorks, in 1861, educated at the Grammar School of that town, at the English College, Lisbon, Portugal, and at a seminary in the United States. The death of his father in 1879 changed the aspect of his career and necessitated the adoption of some means ot livlihood. He returned to his native town, but left again for a brief experience of theatrical life. Again returning to Bradford, he joined the Borough Police Force, at the suggestion of one of its Superintendents, who was an old family friend. At the early age of nineteen he donned the lamp and helmet and was initiated into the joys and sor- rows of a street Constable's life.

One night,shortly after his appointment, his beat I lay in a remote suburb, and hearing screams at the rear of some aristocratic-looking residences, the young officer hastened to the scene. Two frenzied servant maids outside, and a bedroom in flames, were what he saw. Gathering from the incoherent speech of the girls that someone was yet in the house r.C.Talbot rushed into the building and made his way upstairs, through blinding smoke, into the burning room, to find two little cnildren uncon- scious in their bed. Seizing one in each arm he fought his way back to the open air, safely landed his charges, and then returned with the intention of trying to check the fire. Whilst doing 60 he re- ceived a severe cut in the head from falling glass, and his hand and arms were so severely burned that he will carry to his grave some physical souvenirs of that adventure.

After two years of street duty, P.C. Talbot was transferred to the Detective Department, where he rapidly made his mark. His education, tact, and readiness of resource peculiarly fitted him for his new position. Possessed of an excellent memory, untiring energy and plenty of pluck, he soon be- came a thorn in the side of the local " cross-men." The life of a Detective Officer in a large town teems I with so many startling incidents that it is difficult to particularise, but one or two episodes may be I interesting. One Saturday night, in the worst neighbourhood I of Bradford, a " rough " named Manton brutally I murdered a man in the street, and temporarily made good his escape. The whole Force was at once in a state of feverish activity. Officers were despatched I here, there, and everywhere; the printing press and the telegraph had a busy night of it, but Sunday wore to noon with the murderer still at large. About 3 p.m. on the Sunday information reached Mr. Talbot which caused him to believe that Manton was concealed at a certain houQe in a neighbourhood that swarmed with thieves and viclent characters. Accompanied only by a single colleague the young detective visited the district. As they approached the sus- pected house every window and door in the street was filled with villainous menacing faces. Suddenly the officers were electrified to see a door thrown open and their roan dash up the road, bent upon ' making a bold bid for freedom. But fleet as he was he found more than his match in young Talbot, who pressing him hard, forced him to take refuge in an outhouse. Here the culprit assumed a dangerous attitude, but was quickly overpowered and hauled from his retreat. Even then it seemed as though the task of the police must end in failure, for a large crowd of desperate characters collected, threatening the officers and inciting the prisoner to resist apprehen- sion. The fact that most of these cowards were known to the detectives deterred them from open violence, and Manton was safely lodged in the lock- up. The sensational murder at Strangeways Gaol in 1888 brought Mr. Talbot prominently before the public. A notorious burglar named Firth, alias Jackson, etc., after braining Warder Webb with a hammer, daringly escaped from the prison and for weeks eluded the most diligent pursuit. Immediately in many towns in the North burglaries were committed in a manner known to be a favourite one with the fugitive. De- tective Talbot took an intense interest in- the hunting down of Jackson, being in- strumental in procuring and circulating the first photograph of the criminal supplied to the Police after his escape. One of this Officer's duties was to visit the cells at the Bradfnrd headquarters every I morning with a view to spotting old offenders de- tained under assumed names.

One night, when the "Jackson " panic was at its height, a man was locked up in Bradford upon a trivial charge. Re gave the name of Thomas Harrison, and under that designation would pro- bably have passed through the fingers of the Police. had not something peculiar in his appearance at- tracted the special notice of Detective Talbot in the course ot his morning round of examination Questioning the prisoner, Mr. Talbot was informed that he (Harrison) was a joiner lately returned from a long residence in Philadelphia.U.S.A.Knowing something of that city, the officerasked the prisoner how far Kensington (a Philadelphian suburb) lay from the city proper. " Harrison " replied that he did not know, and broke down utterly in reply to several similar questions. Then Mr. Talbot, placing his hands upon the prisoner's shoulders, said to him impressivel3, " I know who you are; you are Jack- son the Strangeways murderer." " God help me," cried the wretched man, falling backwards, "I I am." The news of the capture spread rapidly, and Brad- ford was soon in a state of the wildest excitement. Many refused to believe that the man in custody was the notorious and much-wanted criminal, for many and various had been the "Jackspns " who had surrendered or been arrested during the recent "reign of terror." But the arrival of the man's brothers from Bristol, and their interview with him, allayed all doubts as to the captive's identity, and a few weeks later Jackson paid the penalty of his crime upon the scaffold. For Mr. Talbot's share in this notable case the Watch Committee of Bradford promoted him to the Merit Class of the Detective Department, and he was en- trusted with the important post of Convict Inspec- tor. The Officer has always been remarkable for his tenacious memory of faces, and for the facility with which he can recognise, either in photographs or otherwise, the lineaments of a person once known to him, no matter how altered or disguised. In 1888 Mr. Talbot successfully competed with a large number of candidates for the post of Inspec- tor of the Lancaster Constabulary, which position he held creditably for two years. He is kindly re- membered by the inhabitants of the "Royal Borough." He was selected in June, 1890, from a large number of applicants, to be Chief Constable of Kendal, being then only twenty-eight years of age. With the inhabitants of" ye old grey town" be is popular and his men highly esteem him Re- peated compliments have been awarded him for the able manner in which he and his force have dealt with and checked the rowdyism formerly preva- lent in the streets of Kendal, and upon the steady decrease of crime and drunkenness in the locality. 'ln the course of a busy life Mr. Talbot has found time to dabble somewhat in literature, and has written a good many sketches, stories, etc., for several popular publications.

div.head: RE WAS SURE OF IT.
div.p: RE WAS SURE OF IT.

A little five year-old lad recently said to his father, " Tommy Brown is going to have a new bicycle." " Ah ! my boy," replied the father, " but Tommy's father surely cannot afford such an expense. What makes you think so ? " " ! but I'm sure he is going to have it because his brother said so, and he knows." Happy boy. The father could say no more. He did not like to teach his boy his first lessson of unSelief. He did not like to tell him that people in this world sometimes make exaggerated or false statements. That in deciding upon all questions one must cultivate that penetration which enables one to discern the wheat from the chaff. So he smiled and said nothing. But the time will come for the lad, as it already has to us, when he must sift and decide for him-elf the good from the bad ; the truth from the untruth. We soon learn that in conversation things are oftentimes hastily and thoughtlessly said that in a moment are regretted, or that would not have been said in a more quiet and thoughtful mood. The only statements that the financial world, in fact the general public, rely upon, are those written and attested in a manner which can be verified and brought home to the writer, and this is why they carry conviction to every reader. Mr.G. Pate, 14, Brook-road, Upper Holloway, London, N., made the following written statement, which he knows to be accurate,and which can be easily verified. It will in- terest every reader, and this is our reason for publishing it. He says :—" My experience with Warner's Safe Pills is so satisfactory that I cannot refrain from making a public acknowledgement. For years I have bee -1 try- ing different kinds of laxatives and pills, but never found anything that suited me until I tried Warner's Safe Pills. My occupation often times exposes me to dangerous and poisonous gases, which escape from drains and pipes, and I require, not only a laxative,but a medicine which will at the same time increase the I circulation and keep the blood pure. These pills are easy to take, leave no bad taste (being sugar coated), and never cause griping. My son-in-law says, if one has a headache he should never 'retire without taking , one or two of these pills at night, which will ensure a ! disappearance of the headache by morning. I have frequently recommended these pills to others, and shall continue to do so whenever opportunity offer. I might add that my sister-in-law received so much benefit from the use of Warner's Safe Cure, that she considers it an invaluable tonic, safe, pleasant, and effective, for ladies.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF COUNCILLOR A. BENNETT AND MISS RICHARDSON.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF COUNCILLOR A. BENNETT AND MISS RICHARDSON.

On Thursday last week at 11.30, a.m. the marriage of Councillor A. Bennett, son of Mr. William Bennett, Lyndhurst, Padgate, to Miss Lily Richardson, eldest daughter of Mr. Edwin Richardson, Paddington House, Paddington, took place at the Padgate Wesleyan Church. The marriage excited great interest among the inhabit- ants of Padgate and the surrounding district and at several places streamers were to be seen flying in hon- our of the event. The wedding party were favoured with beautiful weather, as the day though slightly cold was very fine. The church for a long time before the hour for the performance of the ceremony, was well filled. The organist, Mr. W. S. Woods, previous to the bride entering the church, played the "Bridal March "from Wagner (Lohengrin). On the wedding party entering the church, the choir struck up the hymn "The voice that breathed o'er Eden," a good number of the congre- gation joining. The bride who was attired in white duchesse satin, trimmed with valenciennes lace and orange blossoms and veil, also carrying a lily of the valley rose bouquet with orchids and orange blossoms, was accompanied by four bridesmaids, Miss Edith M. Richardson (sister of the bride), Miss Moreton (cousin of the bride), and Miss Edith Bennett and Miss J. Bennett (sisters of the bridegroom). Miss Richardson and Miss Mlreton were attired in creme cloth, trimmed with green brocaded silk, and the Misses Bennett, in cr6me cloth with pink brocaded silk. They carried bouquets of pink carnations with autumn leaves. The bridegroom's gift to the bride was a pearl and gold necklet, and to the bridesmaids, pearl brooches. The officiating clergy- man was the Rev. T. F. Nicholson, of Oxford (cousin to the bridegroom), who was assisted by the Rev. Owen Watkins, superintendent of the Warrington circuit. The bride was given away by her father, and the best man was Mr. Fraser, of Warrington. After the ceremony was over, the choir sang the hymn " Jesus let Thy blessing rest," and as the party left the sacred edifice,Mr. Woods played the wellknown Mendelssolan's " Wedding March." The wedding breakfast was held at the residence of the bride's father. The heneymoon will be spent at Strat- ford on Avon, Oxford and London. The Westminster'Coroner—beld an:inquest on Wednes- day upon the body of Frederick Miers, aged sixty, a German who poisoned himself on the Thames Embank- ment on Saturday, and read a pathetic letter addressed to him which the deceased had left. The deceased said that for three years he had been fighting for an existence in London, with no money to buy food, and he was starving. He had without avail appealed to wealthy men "who go to church and pull long fapes." A rich German merchant whose aid he asked advised him to go to the Salvation Army workshops. "After three years' struggling," the deceased added, "I find myself a wreck bodily and mentally. In my case suicide is no crime. It is a necessity."

DIMINUTION IN NUMBER OF TENANTS. Several appeals wer made with regard to assessments upon houses in Lwchford. It was stated that there I were far more houses than tenants.—The Chairman said that there wanted a new Ship Canal made to find vrtirk Mr. rateable , Woodcock ' 1; for the people. AN APPEAL BY THE WARRINGTON CORPORATION. Mr. Wow:icons appeared on behalf of the Warrington Corporation to appeal against the assessment of the Old Barracks, %Vilson-Pattern-street. There were three ap peals, on portions of the harracks,assessed at gross £6O, tr rooms at £.24,and £2O 10>.; and warehouse and £l5 10s. With regard to the first appeal, said that was with regard to a small block of buildings en the north side of the barracks. In this part, there was a small guard room, and a series of small. cells. They were practically of no value and were at present unoccupied. They might be used occasionally for band practice. The Clerk : The question appears to be with regard to the value of the property which has been acquired by the Corporation. It would be better to refer the whole question to Mr. Owen.—This was agreed to by the committee.

THE ASSESSMENT OF GOVERNMENT PROPERTY. The CLERK read a letter signed by the Mayor of Ports- mouth, the Chairman of the Pdrtsea Island Board of 1 Guardians, the Chairman of the Portsea overseerSiatid the Chairman of the Portsmouth overseers, in whi3ll they say that in their opinion, government property should be subject to the sarne mode of assessment as other property. They pointed out that the rates as fixed by the govenment were sometimes practically nominal. 1 —The Clerk said that no doubt the letter had been sent owing to the fact that there was government property in the Warrington district. He would ask Mr. Tunstall whether in his judgment the assessment of the govern- ment property at all approached what it would likely be if the property was assessed as other property was.— Mr. Tunstall; We should receive a much larger sum.— The Clerk : In that case it is desirable to instruct me to write to the effect that the Warrington Assessment Com- mittee would take part in any movement with regard to this question.—Mr. Tunstall said that it was claimed that government property could not be properly assessed in the ordinary way, as that land could not be occupied for other purposes.—The Clerk said that it would be well for the committee to take part in the movement as it was stated in some quarters that government property was only assessed at a nominal sum.—The suggestion of the Clerk was agreed to.

- THE VALUER'S REPORT.--THE ASSESSMENT OF PARR HALL. Mr. OWEN said that he had made the fellowing valua- tions :—Parr Hail: He was of opinion that for the present, an assessment might be fixed of gross £2OO, rateable £l7O. Messrs. Armitage and Rigbr, Limited, Cockhedge Mills: gross £2,750, rateable £2,144. This Company appealed in conscquence of their dye works being wholly chsed and stripped. He had inspected the premises and found that the dye works were closed and dismantled. A partial reduction was made for this in August 1893, amounting to gross £l3O, rateable £lOO, leaving on the buildings as warehouses, gross £37, rate- able £3O, which should now be deducted; but in addi- tion to this there were buildings a jining the dye works also closed, consisting oi smithy and mech mica! shop, the assessment on which was gross £26, rateable £l9 103. Adding this to the further deduction to be made on the dye works, a total deduction was arrived at of gross £63, rateable £49 103., which would leave the assessment on the whole works, gross £2,687, rateable £2,094 103. Messrs. Bishop and Co. works in Dial-st., gross £206, rateable £169, appealed against the assess- ment asking for a reduction on the ground that the pre- mises were built in advance of their requirements and were not wholly occupied. He had inspected those pre- mises and found that the last new building which was assessed at gross £63 103., and included in the total VMS part not wholly occupied. He thought a temporary re- duction from the gross of £2O might be made on that account, and he found that between gross and rateable, he had not hitherto given the full 25 per cent, deduction which was allowed to chemical works. If they decided upon the temnorary allowance, the assessment would read, gross £1.86, rateable £145 In Newton, with regard to Mr. William Berry, Legh Arms Hotel, the Committee decided to follow the Income Tax Commissioners, and to reduce the assessment from gross £l3O to gross £llO, rateable £93 103. In Haydock, the Infectious Diseases Hospital, St. Helens Corporation was assessed at gross £62, rateable £so.—The report was adopted and it was pointed out that the assessment on Parr Hall was only fixed at the above rate for the present. This concluded the business.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

A Barrow correspondent stateg that there is a pros- pect of a settlement of the labour troubles in the steel trade there. The directors of the Barrow Steel Company are willing to reopen their works if the men will start on the terms of the "Jeremiah Head award," with a pros- pective increase in wages of 5 per cent. It is believed that the men, who number 1,200, will accept the offer, as much distress exists.

The police were infornsed on Wednesday of a terrible tragedy which took place in Manchester on Tuesday night. Mrs. Rourke, a teach,ir of dancing, residing in Nelson-st., and widely known under her professional name of Madame Elene Webster, administered poison to her two boys, one aged eleven and the other eight, and then by the same means took her own life. The younger of the boys seems likely to recover.

The Public Prosecutor, after a consideration of the evidence relative to the Morecambe pier disaster, is of opinion that it does not j i,tify criminal proceedings being taken against anyone in respect of the deaths which oc- curred through the collapse of the landing-stage. In Salford County Court on Wednesday his Honour Judge Parry gave judgment for ten guineas and costs against a cyclist who had knocked down and seriously injured a young girl in Deansgate. His Honour in giv- ing judgment said "it was a very unfortunate thing that there were bicyclists who seemml to think that the whole of the road was made for them. They brought into con- tempt and disgrace the large number of people who rode without interfering with the comfort and pleasure of others."

div.head: READ WHAT THEY SAY:-
div.p: READ WHAT THEY SAY:-

One of those modern monstre establishments, whose re- sources are so boundless, and whose stocks are so comprehen- sive, that it can, with equal care and despatch, furnish throughout a cottage or a mansion, is to be found in the famous house of J. GRIISHON, fuinishing contractor of 44, Oldham-street, Manchester. This Colossal business was commenced in 1870, and being conducted with remarkable ability, energy, and foresight, and on sound commercial principles, It rapidly grew in public favour and patronage until at the present time it, is the largest and most represen- tative house of its kind in Manchester. Mr. Gershon at- tends to evek7 customer personally, and does not leave cus- tomers in the hands of salesmen. Operations are carried on in a magnificent block of four-storey buildings, occupying a prominent and attractive position, and having a splendid frontage, They comprise shops, offices, and capacious show- rooms on the ground floor, and further suites of extensive showrooms on the first, second, and third limes, togethes with showrooms at the rear of vast capacity, and filled to re- pletion 'with an immense collection of valuable goods. Mr. Gershon is a thorough exponent of the general house furnishing, ana stocks held are unrivalled in Manchester, either in magnitude, variety, or worth ; if wide experience and far-seeing policy are absolutely requisite in properly selecting and getting together such a stupendous conglomer- ation of miscellanems goods, it is equally true that, a great amount of ability of no common order is necessary to arrange and group them with such admirable effect, and to maintain at the same time such regard for the comfort and'convenience of visitors. Where everything that can possibly be considered to belong to this branch of business is fully represented, it is an endless task to attempt anything like an enumeration in detail, it will be sufficient to indicate the leading lines with which the house Is occupied. Superb and comprehen- sive stocks are held in Drawing, Dining, and Breakfast Room Suites, made of all the best woods, artistically elegant in design, and magnificently and gorgeously upholstered in all materials of various colours, shades, and tints. Bedroom Suites made of the most dainty materials, and of the choicest patterns. And substantial, solid-looking Library. Stuely, and Hall Furniture, together with inex- haustible supplies of splendid couches, ottomans, and so as, duchesse stands. siciebo..rds, book-cases,cheffoniers, cabinets, Davenports, easy, occesional, and other chairs, dining tables, dressing, work, card lon, a d occa,lonal tables, whatnots, overmantels, chests of drawers as well as a large assortment of bedsteads of every deseription, p ttern, size and price ; bedding, mattresses, curtains, fenders, fireirons and carpets, rugs, and mats of every pattern and design, from all the most celebrated makers. Briefly, the stock embraces every article of whatever kind that can possibly be required in furnishing any or every kind of residence, from the cottage to the mansion of the noble; and not only is each in- dividual article to be found in these marvellous stores, hut each article is represented by a large collection, often unique In its kind, and including a wide selection in style: quality, and prices. This enterprising firm have also manufacturing -premises of considerable extent, and thoroughly equipped with plant and machinery of the newest and best kind and 1 a large number of skilled workmen are constantly employed !in the ma mfacture of cabinet work of all descriptions. Repairs, too, are executed on the premises, a little army of assistants is employed in the control of this stupendous establishment., and competent men are sent all over the kingdom to fit up private residences, hotels, offices, public buildings, and mansions, in conjunction wi h their businese, The connection of this representative house is far-reaching and most valuable, its goods !save acquired the highest repu- tation in Lancashire and the neighbouring counties, and the name of "Gershon "is an ample guarantee for everything that is super.or to his line of business. The proprietor is a man of extensive experience and or great and varied know- ledge in the various branches of the business in Which he is engaged. His able and energetic supervision is given to the whole of the concern, and the utmost vigilance is used that nothing shall emanate from his establishment which shall tend to detract from the high and well-merited reputation the firm has achieved. Mr. Gershon is held in great esteem in private life for his ability, public spirit, and commercial integrity. We strongly advise those about fernishing to call at Mr. GBIISHON'S Universal burnishing Arcade, 44, • OLDHAM - STREET, ANCM MTH a. • (Next door to the Adelphi Bank).

Tux trial or exhibition of horse- Carriages. less carriages which was held at Tunbridge Wells on Tuesday was in its way a very notable event. A few weeks ago an interesting article appeared in the "Field" on "The Passing of the Horse" in America in which "le writer showed that thousands of horses had Within 'the last few years been displaced on American tramways by electric and other modem , Methods of propulsion. When the class of carri- ages which were shown at Tunbridge Wells come extensively into use the "passing of the horse" will be more complete than ever. That useful quadruped will be displaced not °IIIY from tram-lines but also to a large extent from the streets and highways. As one writer who Saw Tuesday's exhibition says, "if present hopes are realised, we may find carriages without horses careering-, not wildly, but soberly and, steadily along the highways throughout the country." These horseless vehicles are, it appears, not the novelty that might be imagined. They simply afford ell Other illustration of the adage that there is 17*thing new under the sun. So far back as 1834 steam coach styled the" Era" ran from Pad- uington to the City of London carrying fourteen Passengers at the rate of sixpence a head. Nit in 1834 the hour had not come for horseless oar- jagels, not on the highways at all events. The enthusiasm of the innovators of that day was ab- Sorbed by the railways, and later on another ha- Peliroent was thrown in the way by the passing of ;the Highways and Locomotives Act- which l lelited the spiel of seK-propelled vehicles to two miles an hour and furtlx3r enacted that there must be two men in charge while a third walked a ce rtain distance in advance carrying a flag of s,"anger. The Act was, of course, framed with a 2ewito regulate the movements ot the unwieldy 7a, eGion-engine, but it has been held by legal au- bawlorities to apply to even a tricycle with steam c,°tive power. But that Act will, it may be con- muently ezpected, be revised now that ordinary eZriages can be driven withou t the aid of horses. ,_ae carriages that were exhibited at Tunbridge ells were propelled by petroleum engines didered very little in - outward _PPearance from the ordinary broughams, tiP.ntetons and other vehicles in• everyday use, ealpt that they are fitted with wheels of the firleYnle pattern with rubber tyres. The engines tie Placed on the front or at the back of the car- and they are, it is said, of pretty much the 7lne type as the ordinary gas engines, except that AaPorised petroleum is used in place of coal ga3. Zni_. average speed of eight miles an hour is obtain- :4e, though a maximum of fifteen miles can be 7aChed if desired. The cost of working is about third Of a penny per mile, and enough oil can 200"" carried for a journey of from 150 to railes. There is evidently a future for these tro-ovlsl vehicles though the present price— £2oo to £3oo—is almost prohibitive.
