THE THEFT OF FOWLS AT SUTTON,

- _ At Knutsford Quarter Sessions, Alexander Jackson, labourer, was found guilty of stealing a cockerel and two pullets, the property of Hannah Bate, at Sutton, on the Bth September. Mr. Lance Bentley prosecuted, and Mr. Latham defended.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for three months hard labour. WESLEYAN MISPON. NELSON-STREET.. .

A well-attended Rower service was held in the Nelson street mission-room an Sunday evening. Mr. Hill delivered an address, and the choir sang several selec- cl tions. Mr. E. Egerly was the accompanist. The flowers were aft3rwards distributed to sick persons, and inhabitants in the vicinity of the mission. HOLY TRINITY CHURCH CHOIR. RUNCORN.

1 In connection with this choir, a soc;ial gathering was held on Friday evening in the Infant's schoolroom. The programme provided by members of the choir and friends consisted of songs,part songs, trios, and duets. During the evening refreitiments were handed round, and a number of games were indulged in. Altogether a most enjoyable time was spent. " VOLUNTEER SOCIAL CLUB, RUNCORN. At the outcome of a billiard match between sides chosen by Mr. Tom Jones and Mr. John Widdows, con- tested at the Volunteer Social Club, a considerable num- ber of members sat down to an excellent hot-pot supper on Friday evening, and subsequently sevsral hours were spent in an enjoyable manner under the presidency of Mr. F. Wiswall. Songs, sentimental, patriotic, and humorous. wers given by Messrs. J. Booth, W. L. Elli- son, A. Crosby, J. Widdows, W. Wright, and Colour. Sergeant Poole. Mr. C. LeCouteur kindly acted as ac- companist and performed several selections. Two items that highly delighted the company wore recitations by Mr. C. Chanter.

div.head: BILLIARD MATCH.
div.p: BILLIARD MATCH.

A number of members connected with the Liberal Club, Runcorn, proceedod to Chester on Wednesday afternoon for the purpose of competing against the Übe. ral and Counties Club of Chester in a game of billiards. The afternoon was spent in an enjoyable manner, some going as far as Eaton Hall. The game was well contested, Runcorn winning eight games to four. The Chester team, however, won by two points. INTERESTING PRESENTATION TO A FORMER RUNCORNIAN. Mr. James S. Boot°, now of Edinboro', son of Mr. T. Boote, of Leinster Gardens, was on Tuesday even- ing the recipient of a handsome present on the occasion of his marriage. It consisted of a silver salver and silver tea service and the inscription ran as follows. :—" Pre- sented to service, S Boute by the Brethren of the Lodge St. David, No. 36, Edinboro', OR the occasion of his, marriage, as a token of the esteem in which he is held, and as a recognition of his valuat,:e service as office bearer, particularly as senior wardeo. June,1895." The presentation was made by the Wor-iiipful Master in the presence of a large company. Mr.]; Jote was still further surprised when he was handed a I.autiful gold bracelet, set in the centte with diamonds, for his wife. SAD DEATH OF A YOUTH AT RUNCORN.

About eight o'clock on Thursday morning, a youth, 15 years of age, named Thomas Jones,soil of Mr. Frank Jones, of 19, Criselton-road, Chester, was found dead in bed at the house of . Gleave, 4, Surrey-St., Runcorn. Deceased travelled with Messrs. Peak Frean, and Co.'s biscuit vati,and arrived in Runcorn on Wednesday Be retired to rest at the house mentioned about 10.30 on Wednesday night, and on Miss Gleave knocking at his bedroom door on Thursday morning she received no re- sponse. Her mother subsequently went into the room and shook the lad,and then discovered that he was dead. He had had as a bed-mate a young Ivan named Arthur Pye who did not notice anything unusual when he went to his work early in the morning. The deceased's brother visited Runcorn on Thursday, night and identi- fied him. He said that his brother had enjoyed good .health, but for the last fortnight be had been troubled with a cough. _An inquest will be held on Friday.
BRIDGEWATEr' R CHANGES' AND THEIR EFFECT ON RUNCORN.

It is reported that the Bridgewater trustees contemp- Plate making a number of important changes at their Worsley yard. They purpose removing their forges and mechanics shop from Worsley to Walkden, and it is pro- bable that they will establish the depot which was at Worsley in the days of the old Duke of Bridgewater and has been retained down to the pre-ent time, at Walk- den, and that the Manchester Ship Canal Company will utilise toe Woreley yard with a view to the relief of Run- corn. It is further stated that the trustees intend open- ing a foundry at Walkden in which employment will be found for a number of colliers who have been discharged from the trustees pits. From inquiries, we understand that the " relief of Runcorn " refetred to,will only mean the transfer of the forge at Old. Quay where not more than six men are employed. A LOCAL WATCHMAKER IN TROUBLE. _ _

At Knutsford Qua'ter Sessions on Monday, James Tinsley (24), jeweller, was indicted for converting to his own use a watch, of which he was the bailee, the pro- perty of Edwin Gregory, and thereby stealing the same, at Runcorn, on 12th October, 1894. There was another charge against the prisoner in reference to a watch, the property of William Moores.—Mr. Roberts. who prose- cuted, said the prisoner before September last was in business in Bridge-at., Runcorn, as a joweller. In the ordinary course of business he received a watch from Mr. Gregory for the purpose of repairs. Mr. Gregory applied several times to get the watch back, and he eventually heaid that the man's business was sold, and that he had gone away. About the same time he re- ceived a letter from the prisoner saying that he was sorry to tell him that be had pawned the watch. It was found that the watch had been pledged by the prisoner in the name of John Williams. In answer to the charge the prisoner said it was all through betting. He had lost a lot of money,and he had pawned the watch intend- ing to get it back. The other case against the prisoner was exactly the same as the nne he .had described.—Mr. Yates, who appeared for the prisoner, said his downfall had been caused by betting. He had hitherto borne a good character, and he asked the court to deal with him nder the First Offenders Act.—The prisoner's father ( P.C. Gregory gave evidence as to his previous good criaracter.—The prisoner was-bound over in the sum of £2O, with his father as surety in the same amount, to come up for judgment when called upon. MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN.II The annual harvest festival in connection with the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Mission to Seamen was held on Sunday, and the services were well attended. The church had been nicely decorated for the occasion, and reflected great credit upon the taste and skill dis- played by the following workers :—Mrs. R. Abel, Mrs. Mack, Mrs. H. The communion .table contained baskets of flowers, several plates of fruit, and two large loaves of bread, whilst within the communion rails, the harvest of the sea was repre- sented by various kinds of fi,l/ which had been provided by Mr. George Duckett, of Church-street. The display on the whole was very fine, and was greatly admired. The Rev. A. J. Jameson, MA , was the preacher at the morning service and preached from the text, St. Matthew, xib., 31. !•?.F.itl MIS GAS EXPLOSION AT RUNCORN. A eerioll• • a p,o.,••ii el get', ”t:eurr,i ut I' ie-,ley even- in, at the h.tu,t of Mr. El. Davies, jilner, Eltesine: erst., Runcorn. On retnrning home for tea, Mr. Davies found that there was a strong smell of gas in the house,and had the supply turned off at the meter. Being unable to ascertain die, whereabouts of the leakage, he called in an apprentice gr -litter named Neill, who decided to put some water it' the chandelier in the parlour, and asked for a light to be given him, although questioned as to the desirability of using one. The light seems to have ignited the ascaped gas for a terrific explosion took place. Neill received serious injuries to his face, and it is remarkable that he escaped alive. The lobby wall was entirely %lowa down and the front door was wrenched from its hinges. The windows were smashed and other damage was done to the house. Fortunately the family of Mr. Davies were at the rear of the premises at the time and escaped un- hurt beyond a severs fright. Neill proceeded to Dr. McDougell's surgery where his injuries were attended to. He is now progressing favourably. The explosion was heard for some distance around.—rhe house was in- mired in the Royal Insurance Society,and a representa- tive came to Runcorn on Wednesday, and despite the fact that the damage was done by an explosion, he ad- mitted the claim and gave instructions for the amount of damage to be restituted. TEA AND Comma. IN GREENWAY-ROAD SCHOOL. Their first contribution was "The PinkParasol,"and in this each displayed a Jap- anese umbrella. The other piece given was "We walked." and the children presented a pleasing appearanco their white dresses, red sashes, and snow-white Moth, r Hebbard bonnets. Each item was encored. The chil- dren taking part were Alice Sayles,Maggie Hillidge,Dora Wrson, Lucy Ilitchin, Ada Woodward. Florrie Hill, Linde Saylee, and Bessie Williams. Three recita- tions were given during the evening as follows : " Christmae Day in the Workhouse," Miss Davies ; " Charley Latham's Pard," Mr. Page ; and "The Stationmaster's story," Mr. Hulse. Solos were sung by Mr. Amble:Fe Shingter, Miss Hillidge, Mr. John Stubbs, Miss Wilson, Miss Vernon. Miss Lucy Hitchin, and Mr. Pilgrim. A duet W4ti contributed by Miss dtiflti Davies, and Mr. Ambrose Shingler,and a glee party sang several nieces. Gere'y, Mr. J. Holford. Mr. J. Hot. ford, jun.. Mr. John Minehall, and Mr. R. W. Newell, and all sane in such gond style as to receive hearty re- ceptions. Sutton and Fleming, Peter iiines, an elderly man, was charged with assaulting and beating his wile,Ann Hines, on the 12th October.—Mrs. Hines, who appeared with a bandage round her head, said her husband was a man who never worked and on Saturday night he came home dunk and chased her into the house of a Mrs. Kelly, where he cornered her and struck her on the head with a brick. She was rendered insensible and had to be taken to the Infirmary. She further added that prisoner had not given her ss. in 18 years. She asked to be pro- tected against him and said she coald well do to be separated from him without any allowance.—Sergeant Chantler said he apprehended the prisoner on a warrant in the Market ;nlace,when he was under the influence of drink. He a.- Aitted striking his-wife on the head with a brick and knocking her down. Witness added that complainant was a sober woman.—This was prisoner's 33rd apirarance and he was committed to gaol for two month's hard labour. Complainant was advised to I lock him oat if he same to molest hgr,and if he persisted the magistrates promised to give her protection. How DID HE GET TSB RINGS At the Police Court on Thursday. before Alderman Sutton and Mr. J. H. Fleming, Thomas Quinn, a young man employed as a collier, was charged with offering at Messrs. Morton'a shop, two gold rings in pawn without beingjable to give a satisfactory account of them.—Mr. Pye, manager of the pawnshop, said that at 7.30 on Wed- nesday night the prisoner called at the shop with tws rings and gave the name of Thomas Quinn, 18 Orford-lane. He said he bought °flaring in Barnsley, 12 months ago, and the other was a present. They were worth about ss. 61 each.—Detective-Sergeant Monaghan said on Wednesday night he visited Morton's shop and saw defendant with Mr. Pye. Defendant gave his address, and witness noticing that he had a third ring on his finger, took him to the Police Station. Here he asked him to give a separate account of each ring. The first he said he bought in Barnsley last Monday morning for 64. 6d„and the second he ssid he obtained in Colcnes,:er, from a woman named Nance. When charged he made no reply. Witness pointed oat that both rings were similar, an un- ustial circumstance.—Defendant said if the case was adjourned he could get evidence as to his having come by the rings honestly.—Mr.Hunt said if he left the rings in their possession,and could bring satisfactory evidence to bear out what he had said, they ,would have no objec- tion to bind him over to appear when called upon.—This course the magistrates took, retaining possession of the rings for the time being.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW WORKS NEAR RUNCORN.
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW WORKS NEAR RUNCORN.

With regard to the statement msde in (Air last issue that the Salt Union, Limited, were considering the advisability of commencing the manufacture of chemicals at Weston, and also of extending their Weston salt works, there is little further to report at present. It is understood that the directors of the company had a protracted meeting on Friday last when the matter was fully gone into. Whether any decision was come to, it has not yet transpired. _ _ _ _ _

A great deal has already been written of the pro- jected new works proposed to be built at Weston by the Aluminium Company, Limited, of Birmingham and elsewhere. There is nothing definitely settled upon as yet, but we may state that Mr. Allen, a representative of 'the company, has again been visiting the district during the past week. The company have already secured offer's of land at Weston for the proposed works, and the chief diffi- culty to be got over now, seems to be in connection with way-leaves which will be required over certain land there, should the works be erected. It will be hoped by all well-wishers, of the town and district, that this difficulty may be overcome, and that before long the first brick of the new works will be laid.
••••••••••••••••••• MESSRS. BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO.
AND THE TEES DISTRICT.
REPORTED NEGOTIATIONS FOR THE OPENING OP NEW WORKS.

The" North-Eastern Daily Gazette" states, in con- firmation of an announcement made in the columns of that paper several months ago,that the salt and chemical Industry on Tees-side Is likely soon to be greatly en- larged by the settlement of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co, on the banks of the river. Owing to the concern awakened at Northwich by the announcement, how- ever, it appears that a reassuring explanation was given, to the effect that, while the company had made up their minds to take advantage of the great natural advantages of Tees-aide and make importment developments, they had no intention of even limiting their North which en- terprises. With regard to the probable data of the open- ing of the new works and the site which they may be expected to occupy, the paper goes on to say :—" It is said that negotiations have been practically completed by which Messrs. Bell Brothers aro about to hand over their ammonia works at Port Clarence to the company (Messrs. Brunner. Mond, and Co.), and that a I large area of reclaimed land will also be atquired. It is believed the new owners will take posetisfrioh, and will begin to develop the concern, as from January next. A great development of the salt and chemical trades of Tees-side may be confidently expected as the result nf this new business arrangement. Hitherto the soda ash produced by Bell Brothers has been bought by Brunner,, Mond, and Co. As the brine is secured from the wells of the Salt Union, the development will also advantage- ously. effect that company. Some months ago the United Alkali Company—which includes Tennant's works both on the Tyne and Tees, and All husen's works, also situated on the Tyne and Tees—contemplated erecting an am- monia works on Teesside for the manufacture of soda- ash, and the land has already been marked out at Port Clarence for that purpose."

div.head: FATHER LEN NON SUED AT THE COUNTY COURT.
div.p: FATHER LEN NON SUED AT THE COUNTY COURT.

Father Lennon, Newton-le-Willow , was sued at the Warrington County Court on Thursday before his Hon- our Judge Wvnne Ffoulks. by Stephen George Ward, High-street, Newton-le-Willows, for damages for the de- tention of a receipt for a grave. Mr. Arthur Browne. who represented the plaintiff', said that his client was a fishmonger 'carrying on business at the above address,and the defendant was a well-known clergyman in the dis- trict. The facts were that Mr. Ward had a child which died in April last. The fact that he was a Protestant and his wife a Roman Catholic, was really the Cause of I the whole complaint at the present time. The mother of tie child wished it to be buried in the Roman Catholic churchyard, and Mr. Ward went to see Father Lennon to ask him to find a grave and bury the child. Father , Lenthon gave him a portion of the land for the grave and trrld him he would be charged £3 3s. to include all fees. After the funeral was over,Mr. Ward ask.l for a reeeipt and Father Lennon promised to give him one. Time went on, and, as no receipt arrived, in May the plaintiff wrote a letter to Father I,rinon informing him that he had not yet received the receipt and asking for it to be sent to him. No reply was received to this letter and ano!her letter was then sent, threatening that unless the receipt were sent at once, the matter would he put in the hands of plaintiff's solicitor to obtain what was legally due to him. No answer came to this alse, and Ward i consulted Messrs. Pearson and Ellis, Wigan. These soli- citors wrote to Father Lennon, and in reply Father Lennon said that hut for seeming discourtesy to them he Would have waited with interest the result of the threatened action. He went on to explain that there were certain legal difficulties in the way of his granting a receipt and said that he did not intend give Ward a receipt which was valueless and would have ns legal weight. Ho also said that that was Gra Ant difficulty which had arisen. As Mr. Ward was ors a Catholic defendant would not object, but vavuld have much pleasure in giving the balance to the plaintiff for the single interment of the child. Mr. Ward further !consulted his solicitors, and another letter was received from Father Lennon in reply to a cnmmunici- ation from them in which he said that he was in honour hound to reserve the grave. As Mr. Ward was not satis- fied, he (Father Lennon) held himself free from any obligation, even of honour. He would, therefore, nay the excess of money for the single interment. Mr. Ward was advised by Messrs. Pearson and Ellis that he was entitled to the receipt as had been promised, and the Bishop of Liverpool was written to. At length after a number of journeys to Liverpool and Wigan,a letter was received from the Bishop of Liverpool on September 11, and enclosed in it he found the receipt which his Lord- ship had received from" Dear" Lennon.. Mr. Browne said that they had got the receipt but Mr. Ward oneht to be recompensed for the trouble he had had in getting it. By a new section in the Stamp Act, when a person withholds a receipt for a bill which requires a stamp,he was liable to a penalty of £lO. His client would, how- ever, agree to withdraw the case if Father Lennon made an apology to him for the trouble he had caused. Mr. Ward had been six months in getting the receipt and much trouble had been incurred. If Father Lennon would apologise, he (Mr. Browne) was instructed to withdraw the case.—His Honour : Ido not see that I can do any- thing in the case.—Mr. Browne said that the receipt hail not been received until September, and surely he could sue for detention.—His Honour, however, said that he did not think he could as the receipt was now in the hands of the plaintiff —Mr. Browne said that if a carri- age were detained far six months, damages could he ob- tained—His Honour said that loss might have been sus- tained in that case. In the present case, however,there was no loss, fie would. however. give Mr. Browne leave to withdraw the case. He could allow no more.—Father Lennon complained that plaintiff had never applied per- sonally for the receipt and had written offensively for it. He thought that case was a vexatious action.—Mr. Browne said that his client had applied personally. He also explained that he had not heel] instructed in that case originally.—Father Lennon asked for costs, but his Honour refused to allow any,

div.head: IMPROVEMENTS TO ANEW ROAD. DRAB WARRINGTON.
div.p: IMPROVEMENTS TO ANEW ROAD. DRAB WARRINGTON.

Writing with regard to th'e state of the approaches from the Chester Main Road to the new road leading over the Manchester Ship Canal at the Swing Bridge, Walton Inferior, Mr. Potts, clerk to the Cheshire County

Council, stated that the Main Roads and Bridges Com- mittee had instructed him to ininat6 to the Rural Coun- Oil, and the County Council would be prepared to carry out the improvement at the point in question, and which the county surveyor intimated would cost £133, provided the Rare! Council would agree to contribute the sum of £5O towards the sarnt.—Mr. Jones said in order to test the question he would move that the sum of £5O be contributed towards the cost of the improvement by the Council.—Mr. Wright seconded the proposition. —Mr. Woodward said they had been assured that the work could be done for £3O. He mlved that the Coun- cil perform the work itself.—lt was pointed out by Mr. Baxter that it would be impossible for the Council to do the work itself as part of the road belonged to the County Council.—On a vote being taken the motion was carried.

div.head: HELSBIE WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: HELSBIE WATER SUPPLY.

tA communication was read from Mr. Joseph Jeffs, chairman of the nelsby Parish Council, stating that the resolution passed by the District with regard to the Helsby Water Supply had been brought before the Parish Council at a meeting held on October 2nd. The folio wiug resolution was passed on the motion of Mr. Taylor. seconded by Mr. Briant, " That this Council is ot opinimn that the Helsby and 'District Water Company should have power to lay water pipes on all the roads under, the control of the District , Council, subject to such terms as are usual with water companies." The directors of the company attended after the resolution was passed, and explained the proposed scheme, which Mr. Brandreth approved of, but still expressed his in- tention of opposing the pipes being laid in Alvanley-road. —Messrs. Potts, Potts, and Gardner, solicitors to the Helsby and District Water Company in a lengthy com- munication said they presumed the District Councit,ha.v- ing ascertained that the ratepayers and inhabitants of Helsby were entirely in favour of the Company's scheme, would now grant the Company permission to lay pines along the length of road in respect of which a similar privilege had already been granted to Mr. Brandreth. The fact that a private individual happened to have a line of pipes along a length of road, was not a sufficient reason for the District Council to block, and, in a great measure, spoil a practical and sound scheme promoted by private enterprise for meeting a public necessity.— Mr. Baxter said the County Council had given the same Company permission to lay pipes along their roads.— The Chairman said their Council had given them authority to do so with the exception of one length which Messrs. Brandreth and Company had already laid pipes in. The Helsby Water Company wanted the Coun- cil to extend the grant to cover this same length as well as Messrs.Brandreth and Company.—Mr. Greenway pro- posed that such powers be given them. He was certain that the Company intended to lay the pipes. If they did not obtain permission, they would go on private land. They required water at Alvanley.—Mr. Farrington said a water supply was required at dalvanley, Helsby and Kingsley.—Mr. Derbyshire seconded the proposition. He was ready to designate Helsby as happy Helsby in-as- much as there were two companies ready to supply the inhabitants with water. He wis ed there was similar opposition in Stretton. If he was going to vote for friends he,should vote for Brandreth, but in order that the people of Helsby might have two striugs to their bow for an inadequate water supply he bad great pleasure in seconding the proposition.—Mr. Brandreth said it was a question full of difficulties, and as their perma- nanent clerk was away, he would move an amendment that the matter be adjourned until the next board day. He might say that a circular had been sent out by the Helsby and District Water Company, Ltd., to all the members of the Council excepting himself. Unfortunately he hadn't received one. He thought in that circular, , charges were made against his position on that Board. He had been • guardian for about t welve years, and it said in the circular that he was unwilling or unable to express the opinion of the parish he represented with re- spect to that matter. During the time he had been a member of the Board he thought the members would admit that be had done his duty to Helsby. The circu- lar further said that he was desirous of compelling neighbouring tenants of cottages and other property to take their water so that the expenses Of his private scheme might be reduced. That was charging him with not acting as an honourable man and that he was op- posing the company for his own selfish purposes and his own profit. It was a very serious charge to make, and if the Clerk had been present he should have consulted him on the matter. If the resolution was passed he should submit his resignation to the Local Government Board, and at-lt them to send an Inspectnr down. He would not go into the particulars now, but he did not think that this Helsby and District Water Company should have any more advantages than he had been granted.—M'. Rovlance seconded the amendment, and said bethought Mr. Brandreth came to do his duty to the ratepayers. He did not think that they should allow this Water Cempany-to dictate to them. On be- ing put to the vote the amendment was carried by nine votes to four.

div.head: NUISANCE AT FRODSHAM STATION.
div.p: THE NUISANCE AT FRODSHAM STATION.

A further communicatian was read from Mr. Charles I Linaker, land agent, Frodsliam, stating that there was no abatement of the nuisance arising from bone trucks at Frodsham station, and, if anything, it was on the in- crease. During the past week the stench had been horri- ble. There had been delay in removing the wagons. It was very unreasonable of Mr. Aaron to suggest that those who did n>t like the smell should clear out, He (Mr. Linaker) was not yet in the happy position of Mr. Aaron, who was able to do just as he pleased in a matter of that kind, but one of Mr. Linn ker'a neighbour., who occupied a house at a rateable value of nearly £lOO a year, had" cleared out," and in a great measure his do- ing so was caused by the continuance of the nuisance which behad complained of very frequently. He ven- tured to say that if Mr. Aaron had to eat his breakfast with this delightful odour before him, he would not be long before he was on the track of the offender, and he did not know any per- son who would be so uneasy under such an an Alen as he would be. Mr. Aaron made the state- ment that there was ne money to be got without smell, perhaps this was his idea of the origin of the term 1" filthy lucre." The writer hoped the Authority would not let the matter rest.—Mr. Wood ward moved that Mr. Heywood be requested to abate the nuisance. (Laugh. ter.)—Mr. Baxter seconded. (Renewed laughter.)—Mr. Jones wished to know what course could they take for the abatement of the nuisance. Nothing seemed to be being done in the rratter.—Mr. G. Ashton stated that a solicitor to the company came to see the Clerk, to the Couticil about three weeks ago, and he premised to put the suggestions made for the abatement of the nuisance before the directors of the company. It was probable that they had not met since then.—Mr. Jones wished to- know what the suggestions were.—Mr. Melton said it was intended to put the trucks in another position or to take them to Halton Station, where there were few houses about.—Mr. Jones moved that the Clerk write a strong letter to the railway company urging them to abate the nuisance at once.—Mr. Hoylance seconded the proposition.—Mr. Woodward supported.—Mr. Heywood said a suggestion bad been made that the manufacturers of Frodsham Bridge should apply to the railway company for a siding at Frodsham Bridge. Whether anything would come of it he could not say. If a siding were constructed it wou/d be greatly to the benefit of Frodsham. In addi- tion e the smell from trucks of benes,there were numer- -as trucks of what were known as" Oldham Shoddy."lf the agitation resulted in the closing of any works it would be a great infliction on a number of inhabitants. There were other considerations to be thought of besides the Railway Company. If the comnany could see their way to make a goods station at Frodsharn Bridge it would be a great benefit.—The motion was then carried.

div.head: TAXATION OF BICYCLES.
div.p: THE TAXATION OF BICYCLES.

The Chester Rural District Council submitted the fol- lowirg resolution for the adoption of th• Runcorn Conn- ell "That this Council is of opinion that the time has come when an annual tax of not less than ss. should be put upon all cycles, that such tax be applied to the maintenance of the roads or other taxation; that a number or some other method be adopted for the purpose of registration or identification; and that the County Council be requested to petition Parliament in that behalf." —Mr. Baxter proposed that the Council adopt the resolution. He looked upon cycliFta AA a nuisance to everybody else who used the roads. There was of course a number of respectable men amongst them, but there was also a lot of blackguards. Q Ate recently he had a teamsman very much abused because he did not leave room enough on the roan for three cyclists to pass abreast. One of them jumped off his machine and knocked the man in the fence.—Mr. Weir seconded.— Mr. Woodward took exception to the remarks of Mr. Baxter, concerning cyclists generally. But bethought it only fair that those who used the roads to such a large extent,' should pay an amount towards the taxation of the county.—Mr. Fieywood wished to know what differ- ence there was between a cydlist and a man cn horse- back. The latter was not called upon to pay anything. He did not see why cyclists should te taxed; more than
'-rsemen, espeoi-illy attct nn t rlo the sligh,est

'nage to the roads. He moved Vl:a the commutocation lie on the table as he objected to a tax being put on whit was a recreation throughout the country. They might as well include perambulators. (Laughter. )—Mr. Farrington Said in some places they were making cycle tracks, and it would be wellif the cyclists were made to keep to them.—Mr. Wright seconded the amendment.—Mr. rat- hot, J.P., stated that riders of horses were generally those who contributed to the rates in some ot;ler way, whereas cyclists seldom did.—Mr. Roylance also spoke, and the motion was carried, the mover and seconder ot the amendment only voting against.

BAD ROADS NE-AOL -WARRINGTON. Mr. J. Charlton Parr, Grappenhall Heyes. wrote" May I ask whether the nPw road leading from the high level bridge at Latchford to Wash-lane, Latchford, is under the jurisdiction of your highway authority ? It is in a very bad state with loose stones and requires prompt at- tention. If it is not your road I will apply to the County Surveyor. Nothing has been done at Lumb Brook bridge yet. I think ycu should threaten proceedings if the !Ship Canal Company will not iecognise their liability and do the needful."—Mr. Swinton said the first- mentioned road would be within the Warrington Borough Extension Act. The road did not belong to them. With reference to the road at Lumb Brook Bridge, nothing had been done to remedy it as yet. On the 26th Sep- tember he received a letter from the Manchester Ship Canal Company stating that the material required had been ordered. The Company appeared to be waiting for the material still.—lt was decided that Mr. Swinton shoal again write to the Ship Canal Company stating that the public were complainitg a the state of the road.

HANGING-ROCK-ROAD, HALTON. A communication was read from the Parish Council of Halton, referring to the bad condition of the Banging- rock-road, at Halton. Mr. Wright said it appeared to have been the road to the old castle. It was out of con- dition some years ago and the Duchy of Lancaster re- paired it.—The cmsideration of the matter was ad- journed, it being thought that as the read.chd not belong to the Council, they were unable to deal with the matter.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. Adams reported that a fresh case of diphtheria had occurred at Newton-by-Frodsbam. rwelve cases of scarlet fever had occurred at Norton. The infection was attributed to Darrsbury schools. Two cases of scarlet fever had also occurred at Keckwick, and the spread of the disease was etributed to the same cause. In con- sequence of the extension of the outbreak being trace- able mainly to infection from Daresb ,ry schools he re- commended that the school be closed for a period of one month.—The report was adopted and it was decided that the schools at Daresbury,Moore, and Eiatton should be closed.

div.head: NUISANCE INSPECTOR'S REPORT.
div.p: NUISANCE INSPECTOR'S REPORT.

Mr. Farrington reported that he bad received a letter from Mr. Marshall, secretary to the Runcorn Urban Council. acknowledging the receipt of the repsrt for three analyses of water, and stating that he was puzzled to know why they were sent. There was no organic matter in the water,but it was stated to be hard. Before the samples were sent the reservoir at Halton had been cleansed. The Inspector stated that the reservoir which was in a very flirty condition had been cleansed, and he would take further samples at an early date. This concluded the business.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A meeting of this Board was held at Duttotit Work- house on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Knowles presided, and in addition to the members of the Rural Council being present there were the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi,Mr.A.R. Norman, Mr. S. Yarwoqd, and Mr. G. Ashton (clerk), and Mr. Cunnah (workhouse master).

THE RUNCORN VACANCY. A requisition signed by Messrs. Yarwood and Thomas Lea, members of the Board, had been presented to the Clerk, asking him to forthwith proceed to hold an election to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Thomas Handley, the member for the Heath ward of Runcorn.—The Clerk stated that the necessary notices would be prepared for issue at once.

div.head: WORKHOUSE EXTENSIoNB.
div.p: THE WORKHOUSE EXTENSIoNB.

In accordance with notice of motion given, Mr. Hey- wood moved that the Guardians consent to the expendi- ture of a sum not exceeding £26 in connection with the erection of a casual ward for females in addition to the £335 authorised by the Local Government Board to be expended for that purpose. He further mOvea a resolu- tion authcrising the borrowing of the sum.—Mr. Wcod- ward seconded, and it was agreed to.

div.head: FIRANCE.--COMPLAINT Or REMOVE ;CHARGES.
div.p: FIRANCE.--COMPLAINT Or REMOVE ;CHARGES.

Mr. Hevtvood submitted the report Of the Finance Committee. Quarterly accounts amounting to £1,264 Ils. 7d. were recommended for payment. The balance at the bank was £1,944 83. Bd. Mr. Woodward seconded the adeption of the report.—Mr. Derbyshire said he would like the committee tee exercise a much stricter supervision over the accounts. He noticed that they had two or three printers going. Oae had sent in a bill for over 212, and there was another bill for over £7.— The Chairman called upon Mr. Derbyshire for some ex- planation as to the arms he referred to,but be refused to give any information,and said if he was not in order he would sit down. In answer to an interruption by Mr. Woodward, Mr. Derbyshire said he thought he had a right to speak on the matter and give his opinion. He was proceeding to speak again when Mr. Woodward rose to a point of order, and said the charge made by Mr. Derbyshire was not correct. There was one account for the Board of Guardians and the other for the Rural Council. —Mr. Derbyshire again rose to speak, when the Chair- man wished to know whether he was speaking of the Board or the District Council.—Mr. Derbyshire said he wanted to recommend nothing respecting the District Council. He wanted to remind them that there was not sufficient supervision of the accounts coming before the Finance Committee. He would like to have a little more strict supervision over many of them. He thought there were some rather excessive charges.—Mr. Hey- wood said he did not think Mr. Darbyshire wag right in making the charge that there were overcharges. They hi.d passed an account for Mr. Woodward for 2i 13e.41. and for Mr. Bellamy of £l4 is. id., and both were for stationery. He WAII not aware of any two accounts for one firm. If he had an accusation to make he should give them some details.—Mr. Dirbyshire said he had no accusation te bring against any individual, hut against tho,o persons round the table. There should be stricter supervision of the accounts. The minutes were then passed.

div.head: FIRING A GUN IN A FRODSHAM STREET.
div.p: FIRING A GUN IN A FRODSHAM STREET.

Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas at Frodsham Police Court on Monday morning, William Hayes was charged with being drunk whilst in possession of a loaded gun on Siturday evening and also with wantonly firing the same 6rl the highway.—Samuel L. Hasselton, of Bridge-street. Frodshatn, deposed thst about 2.30 on Saturday afternoon he was standing out- side his house when he saw the prisoner with a gun in his hand, talking to a man named William Jones, the conductor of theltrodshans Town Band. He heard Jones tell the prisoner that he could not shoot, .and he would let the prisoner have a shoot at him, 60 yards away. Jones measured the distance, then put up WS hat, and the prisoner fired, but fortunately the shot struck the ground. There were many children playing about at the time.—Thomas Entwistle stated that he was driving through Newtown when hesaw the prisoner in possession of a gun. Jones was talking to him, and he afterwards saw him measuring some distance.. Witness at the time was between the two of them. The moment he had passed he head a gun fired. His hove jumped but he ' managed to pull up within a few yards, and on looking round be saw that the prisoner had fired ,at Jones, but missed him. The. prisoner was drunk and could not stand or hold his gun steaely.—.Tohn Banks. of Weston,also gave evidence and stated that he was going up Brides-lane with a pony' and trap when he saw the prisoner fire a gun. The pony plunged forward, and came into contact with a lamp-post, smashing the splashboard of the trap. If the pony had not been pulled up in this way the result would have been very serinus indeed to the occupants of the trap.—P.C. Breeze spoke to apprehending the pri- soner, and he acknowledged having fired the gun off. Re was drunk at the time he was locked up.—The prisoner stated that he was coming from the bridge when he met Jones who made a remark to him that he could not shoot him at sixty yards distance. Aker measuring the &s- -tance, Jones held up his hat, and witness fired in order to frighten him but not to hurt him.—The Chairman said they considered the act not only foolish but very dangerous, and Hayes had rendered himself liable to be placed in a serious position. Ha would .be fined 51. for drunkenness or seven day's imprismfnent, *nn 109. and costs or 14 day's imprisonment for firing off the gun. Be might look upon it that they had taken a very lenient view of the ease.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

A BOY'S DISHONESTY—" RELIEVING THE TILL." On Friday, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, before Messrs. Alderman Harrison, Councillor Roberts, and Mr. S. Wright, Joseph Robertson (13), 70, Mersey, atreet, was charged with stealing from a till on the pre- mises of Messrs. W. P. and W. Skelton, in the markot, Md. on Wednesday, is. 34d. on Thursday, and is. on Friday morning.—The defendant pleaded guilty to each charge.—Mr. S. Hunt said that the lad, who was nearly 14,had been employed be the firm in question for about 12 months and was looked upon as trustworthy, but for the last eight or ten days, cash had been missed from a patent till on the Market Hall premises. The Matter was reported to the police and Detective Mona- ghan took it in hand. On Wednesday Md. was missed but that money was unmarked ; on 1 hursday is. 34d. was taken, marked; and on Friday is. Sid. taken, also marked money. Yesterday morning (Friday), Mr. Top- barn, the caretaker opened one of the Hall doors and then went round to open the other. Detective Monaghan and Mr. Earles were on the watch and saw Robertson enter and put his hand into the till, which he prevented from ringing as it otherwise would have done. He put the money in his pocket and the officer then went up and took him into custody. When charged at the Police Station he made no reply with reference to the last offence, but for Thursday he said he took 9d., and admitted taking Md. on Wednesday. Previously, the defendant hid a good character.—After Alderman Harrison had pointed out to the lad the seriousness of big offence, he was ordered to receive six strokes of the birch and be detained at the Station until 6 o'clock at night.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT.
IjATlTßDAy.—Before Mr. John Fairclough (chairman), and

Mr. S Weight. - THEFT OF A PINT OF WTI'S/CF.—Patrick McCue, 9 Bake- tense-yard, Latchford, was charg,d with steeling from the 4' Lower Angel," Buttermarket-street, on Friday afternoon. a pint of wnisky value 28. 21.. the property of Messrs. Peter Walker and bons.—Mr. S. Hunt said the coinplainants were represented by Edwin White, barman of the " Lower Angel" public-house, Buttermarket-street. About 2.30 on Friday afternoon the defendant was in the vaults in question where White was engaged bottling whisky. The bottles were 'placed on a deleboard inside and beneath the counter and were there left while White went down in the cellar for come Peer. When he returned. a few seconds later, he missed one Or the pint bottles and also noticed that defendant and another man h•cl disappeared. White ru-hel to the door and met defendant and the other man coming down the entry from the sii;le door, with something bulky under his Coat. The barman went to him and defendant retreated into the vaults but White, seizing him. said" I want the pint of whisky you have got." Defendant immediattly produced It. and said" We only did it for a 'Ark." White, however, gave him into the custody of P.O. Woods who conveyed the defendant to the police Station. Here when asked to account for the bottle being in his 'accession defen lant said " I found it in the urinal " When charged he replied" I did not steal it, I found it."—Edwin White, barman, in corrobora- tion, said he left six bottles under the counter when he went down the cellar and found only Bye woen he returned. De- tendant had not had time to go to the urinal, so that his state- ment fell through —P.C. %,‘ oods having supported the evi dence, the magistrat.s sent the d fendant, who gave the same excuse about finding the whisky. to gaol for 14 days Lard labour.

div.head: SHALL RAILWAY CROSSINGS BE ABOLISHED?
div.p: SHALL RAILWAY CROSSINGS BE ABOLISHED?

The danger incurred by foot passengers and railway servants at level crossings raises from time to time the question whether, after all, hay& crossings, or places where the high road intersects the railway track, ought not to be abolished, and a bridge or subway made obligatory. . _ .

A danger of quite another kind than that of passing trains, and from which a signalman's wife had lately a fortunate escape, has just been investigated by the " Bridgwater Mercury," and Mrs. Lane, Cokesley Level Crossing, near Wells, Somerset, told all about it. Her danger arose in the first place from a very simple cause —a fit of indigestion ; but it entailed twenty years of suffering, from which she has only lately been relieved. She was so ill as to be totally unable to perform her household duties. She had also spasmodio attacks two or three times a week,which left her so weak in her head that her memory was affected and she could remember scarcely anything—in fact, she was so ill, and suffered so acutely from the three combined causes—indigestion, liver complaint, and spasms—that her life was a perfect misery. She was obliged to warn her husband she was going to die ; the neighbours also thought she could not possibly live. She was attended by a very skaful doc- tor, hut his treatment failed to cure her or to relieve her sufferings to any extent.

prolonged assault ,on the Widnes goal Sharp secured a THE LATE WARRINGTON POSTMASTER. third try, which was improved. Tbe remaining stages ot the game were in favour of the visitors, who won by two goal, two tries (15 points), to Widnes one goal (five points.) WAIMINGT.OK " " V. Sr. HELENS" A ".—Spectators at the wilderspool enclosure on Saturdav were treated to a display of football entirely unlomied for. It was thought that the St. Helens "A " would prove worthy opponents and not that they would allow themselves to be beaten by 40 points to nil. The visitors arrived late and it was not till 4.20 that the game was commenced with St. Helens defending the pavilion goal and with a strong 'wind in their favour. Early ir the game War- rington showed their superiority, (rosier and Edelsten exchanging with advantage. Hoyle kicked into touch near the right-hand corner of the visitors' half and from the ensuing line-out Foster crossed the line at a jump. Price neatly converted into a goal. Scholtz charged the kick-off and Price passed to Lawless who was knocked ' into touch. After a scrimmage the same two exchanged again and the latter after a short run passed in the nick of time to Carey who scored. The kick at goal failed. Scrimmages and line-oura next held swat, and the St. Helens forwards at last broke away only to be checked by Edelsten. Scholtz again got away but was floored without the ball and a free-kick granted Warrington. This failed,and Foster and Edelsteu were instrumental in relieving a dangerous position. From this point War- rington kept up the pressure, Lawless, Foden and Carey, repeatedly breaking away. Price scored from a scrim- mage near the line and Lawless failed at the kick. A moment later Price again secured and passed to Carey who ran nearly half Liao field and again scored, Foden converting. This completed the first half of the match with Warrington leading by 2 goals 2 tries 16 points) to nil. St. Helens re-started, but against the wind made a weaker stand than before, and the home- stirs were soon close on to their opponents' 25 flag, which nositinn they with little change, maintained. Almost at once Foden, Price, Edelsten, and Carey made rapid exchanges, with the result that the latter again scored. This try was unconverted and the next moment the two full backs exchanged kicks, Chadwick tempora- rily relieviag. Lawless was the next contributor to the list of tries being quickly followed by Hoyle. Both were unconverted. Scarcely had St. Helens recovered from their astonishment before Lawleas' amid loud cheers and laughter, crossed the line again and circled round to the back of the goal. From a centre kick Edelsten converted this into a goal. Foden and Price exchanged passes,and the latter seeing an opportunity placed Carey again in possession, and another try was the result. Lawless was successful at goal. Soon alter, a passing movement was initiated, which without a break went along the whol e line of halves and threequarter backs, putting the players very close up. Scholtz scored the final try from a pass by Foster and Edelsten kicked the goal. This brought about" time "and the game ended with Warr- ington winning an exciting gams by 5 goals 5 tries to nil.
INTERESTING PRESENTATION.

There was an interesting gathering of post office offi- cials and employe, in the Warrington Consef vative Assembly Rooms, Sankey-street, on S4turday evening, the occasion being a presentation to Mr. Kerry, the late postmaster, who has severed his connection with War- , rington to take up a more responsible post at Stoke-on- Trent. In all about 150 were present ; including Mr. and Mrs. Kerry, Mr. West (the new postmaster), Dr. Starkey Smith (medical officer for the Warrington post office district),lVlr. Broadhurst (chief clerk), Mr. Bennett (superintendent), Mr. Gorton (telegraph depaztment), Mr. Mellor (inspector of postmen), Miss Richards (mar- ket place branch office), Mr. Hallows (Stockton Heath) Mr. Gleave (Moore), Mr. White (Helsby), and Mr. Clark Orford-lane branch office.) A number of largo plants) nicely arranged on the platform made a pleasing effect. Near to, were the presents to be given to Mr. Kerry. They consisted of two handsome mahogany lounge chairs, manufactured by Messrs. R. Garnett and Sons, Sankey-t. They were upholstered with saddle bags, filled in with Utrecht claret velvet. In addition there was a splendidly carved barometer, supplied by Messrs. William Woods and Sons, Sankey-st. Prior to the com- mencement of the proceedings a number of lively tunes were played by the Post Office brass band, under the leadership of Mr. Parker. A proposition made by Mr. Bennett, seconded by'Mr. Gorton, that Mr. West take the chair was agreed to. - .

The CHAIRMAN then called upon Mr. Broadhurst to make the presentation. Mr. BROADHURST explained that the meeting would have been more largely attended, especially by the sub- postmasters, had it been possible to arrange a more con. venient day, but the committee could not do so, because Mr. Kerry left Warrington earlier than was at first anti- cipated, and could not leave his new duties at Stoke-on- Trent on any other day than Saturdsy. He (Mr. Broadhurst) had received letters of apology expressing regret for inability to attend from many of the sub- postmasters and from some members of the staff, many of ehom were on duty, some away,and, he regretted to say, a few on sick leave. The unanimous expression of all was that it would have given them very great plea- sure indeed to have been with them. When the news became known that Mr. Korry was to leave Warrington, it created considerable surprise and depression, because they all felt that they were to lose a postmaster whose sense of juStice had always been tempered by kindness, and who had always worked with them in such a man- ner as to earn the respect and esteem of them all. (Ap- plause.) The feeling soon vented in a tangible form, and had led to that meeting. There never was a more spontaneous desire than was evinced by all to recipro- cate the kindness which had been shown by Mr. Kerry ever since he came amongst them. Of course he did not wish it to be understood that they had been reclining on a bed of roses whilst Mr. Kerry had been with them ; he knew how to introduce the thorns as well as most people did when it suited his purpose, but if the thorns had occasionally been applied they had been needed just to prod them along and put a bit of spring,as it were,into them. He ventured to think that they were none the worse for the scratching. (Laughter.) He did not wish to prolong his remarks by going on to say what Mr. Kerry had done for them. They all knew quite as well as he did. But it might not be altogether uninteresting if the 7 looked back a little and tried to realise a few of the many improvements which had been instituted. They knew when Mr. Kerry came to Warrington, their work had been going up by leaps and bounds and con- tinued to do so. No revision of the force had been attempted for some time. There was much dissatisfac- tion,and the feeling began to be openly expressed. Mr. Kerry immediately set about the revision with a courage that was worthy of him, and he soon established the work on such a footing as to give the most complete satisfaction. (Applause.) The wants of the public also received a considerable share of attention at this time, and new letter boxes were erected, and later collections arranged,both in the town .and suburbs. He mentioned that as showing the matters Mr. Kerry had on hand whilst he was working so hard to put internal matters right. (Applause.) The first social gathering of the staff was one that would not readily be forgotten. If there was a trace of disaffection remain- ing it was removed; every discordant note gave place to the most complete concord and harmony. Then followed the improved ventilation and lighting of the sorting room, and in short, everything that tended to their com- fort and well-being. There was no wonder that under the improved conditien of things the esprit de corps soon reached a standard of excellence, and its influence would, he was sure, be seen for many years to come. Personally he had always found it a pleasure to work with a will for such an officer as Mr. Kerry had been. He had in- deed been postmaster and friend, and he would always cherish the memory of his too brief connection with them. In his new home he was sure they all wished him success, and their regret did not in the least diminish their congratulations. He had now to ask Mr. Kerry to kindly accept from them two chairs and barometer— (cheers)—as an expression of their sincerest wishes and warmest regares. They had been guided by the desire to present something which should not be merely orna- mental but useful. The Warrington staff heartily joined with him in wishing both Mr.and Mrs.Kerry"God speed" and every success in their new sphere. (Loud applause.) Mr. BENNETT said he cordially agreed with the wards Mr. Broadhurst had given utterance td with regard to Mr. Kerry. He proceeded to speak of the improved arrangements which now existed as the result of Mr. Kerry's management, and hoped Mr. Kerry would live many years to enjoy the comfort of the chairs they were presenting to him. Mr. GORTON thought they all entirely agreed with what had already been said. He spAre of the unique position Mr. Kerry had held, referring to the letter sent him by the Mayor of Warrington, and the entire good- will he had gained of the Warrington staff and of the sub-officers around. Mr. MELLort said he was verfproud to stand up, not only on behalf of the postmen, hut personally to thank Mr. Kerry for the kindness he had exercised towards them. They wished him every success, and trusted that he would make as many good friends in Stoke as he had done in Warrington. Miss RICHARDS said on behalf of the female staff she would like to express how very sorry they were to part with Mr. Kerry. She was sure that since he had been their leader, they had got on beautifully, and there had been much more unity and good feeling amongst the staff, and their work had been quite a pleasure to them. From the first, he seemed to set them at ease by plac- ing every confidence in them when he knew what their abilities were. This seemed to have brought out their qualities, and made them better servants. (Applause.) He carried with him their hearty good wishes, and they hope I that the staff at Stoke would do their best for him, and they were sure, he would be as good to them as he • hailieen to the staff at Warrington. (Hear, hear.) She I would like to give their Chairman and new leader a hearty welcome. (Applause.) She hoped they would go on working as comfortably and well together under his leadership as they had under Mr. Kerry's. (Applause.) Mr. Oxley, Inspector Evans, Mr. Gleave, Mr. White, Dr. Starkey Smith, and Mr. J. Hallows also spoke. In his remarks Dr. Starkey Smith said they were all sorry to lobe Mr. Kerry, but they were pleased to hear of his promotion. He heartily wished both Mr. and Mrs. Kerry every success in their new sphere. Mr. KERRY in acknowledging the presents, said he was deeply sensible of their great kindness, and he thanked them all most sincerely. Such a presentation was be- yond anything he could have expected from them, and to the end of his days he should treasure what they had given him. Nothing could have been more acceptable, and when he relined in one of those chairs he should look back and hear some of the old vo•ces which had been so friendly and kind at Warring- ton. Much had been said about the good he had done for the public service in the town and neighbourhood, but he could not have done it, had it not been for the co-operation of everybody with whom he had come in contact. He had had the most willing and cheerful assistance from everybody. He eould say this that there were very few offices where the public service was carried on as efficiently as in the Warrington office. If the public only knew how thoroughly their work was studied and well-looked after, they would not ofcen corn- plaint. But no expenditure had been incarred which had ' not been well.earned and well applied, end where improvements had been carried out, there the revenue I had increased. It was very hard to say good-bye. He did not know what a beautiful place Warrington was until he left it. (Laughter.) The speaker then pro- 1 ceeded to speak of his work at Stoke and district, and in conclusion he said heleft Warrington conscious of many 1 imperfections, but in the main he had striven to do his best for the Borough, and the district, and the staff, he had had the honour to be connected with so long. (Applause.) In proposing a vote of thanks to the committee, Mr. Kerry said he could assure them that they would have in their new postmaster not only an efficient public officer who would discharge his duty to the satisfaction of everyone in Warringtor, but one who would prove himself willingT to do all he could for the staff with which he worked. (Applause.) Ile was sure they would find him a si ne3re helper and counsellor. With regard to Mr. Broadhurst, he had been told that there was not another chief clerk in Lancashit e as good as him. (Applause.)---Mr. Locker seconded the proposition and it was carried unanimously. Mr.Broad- hurst responded on behalf of the committee, and pro- posed a vote of thanks to the Chairman.—Mr. Bennett seconded.—ln acknowledging the vote, the Chairman said of course he was an untried man in Warrington,and it would be out of place for him at present to say what he should do, or how he should do it. But as an old official he would venture to say with pride and satisfac- tion, that he knew he WAS following a gentleman who had efficiently performed his duties. He paid a high tribute to the admirable arrangements existing at the Warrington office. lii referring to his new appointment he said that since he left Hampshire, the °racing air of the north seemed to have revived his energies, and the past week had been one of surprises to him. An adjournment was afterwards made to en ante- room where tea was provided. Time remainder of the evening was spent in a sociable manner,the proceedings being enlivened by several musical items.

RU BY. TNORTAFtIN ON. WARRING'ION v. ST. OELENs,

The Warrington first team jool aeyed to St. Helens ou Sato tiler to play the first match this season with the senior club of that towa. The Railway Company put on a spacial trait], and some 300 enthusiasts took advant- age of the opportunity of accompanying the team. St.' Helens was leaehed in good time, but it is a weary walk from the station to the football ground, which, though within the borough, is a mile and a half to two miles ' from the siation. However, the Warrliteton enthusiasts, togethe,- with about 3,000 St. Helens peopte, found their way to the ground, and had the pleasure of witnessing a really fiast-class game. Had it been a political election, Warrington would have been said to have won a moral v ietory, that is to say, they ought to have won but they did not. As a matter of fact they did obtain a moral victory, if there can be such a thing in football. They lost miry by a try, but throughout the game they played quite as well as their opponents. and at times had much the best of matters. On the whole we should say that the Warrington team on Saturday was slightly better than the St. Helens team, and had the visitors only had bit of luck they would have won the match easily. Time after time they Made vigorous attacks on the St. Helens line, and just when they seemed sure to score they were repulsed, only to renew the attack shortly afterwards with similar resu:ts. The team generally played a splendid game. The backs were seen to great advantage, though we should have liked to see the two half backs feed the th ree-q LIM ters a little more generously than they did. The forwards worked well together, and played with a spirit which was quite a treat to witness. The St. Helens forwards appeared to pride themselves on the way in which they could "screw" thescrimmage and for a short time they had reason for doing so. But it was not long before the visiting forwards tumbled to the trick, and the "screw " afterwards worked rather loosely, and seldom ended satisfactorily. The referee was Mr. J. El. Potts, of Stockport, and some of the spec- tators commented unfavourably upon some of his deci- sions. The teams were :—Warrington: Full hack, lieesom ; three-quarters, Barber (capt.), Cross, Burton and Broady; half backs, Nevins and Houghton ; for- wards, Burrows, Satioders, Andrews, Barrett, Thornton, Fairhurst, Wilcock and Hill. St. Helens : Full back, Foulkes ; three-quarters, Sudlovv, Appleton, McLees and Doherty; half backs, Little and Ewan; forwards, White- ley. Winstanley, Dale, Rimmer, Caveney, McKay, Briars and Reynolds. It will be seen that St. Helens had the assistance of Ewan, of Salford. The home captain won the toss, and elected to play with a strong wind which was blowing from goal to goal. Nevins kicked off. Ewan gave Little a smart pass,and the ball was carried into the Warrington 25. From the scrimmage, Sudlow passed to Appleton, but Cross in- tercepted and relieved. Sudlow picked up well and kicked, but Beesom by a good mark saved his lines,and shortly afterwards, aided by a useful kick by Cross, Warrington entered St. Helens territory. Free kicks were exchanged, the one by St. Helens sending the ball dead. From the drop out, Briers passed across the field, but Burton gat possession and dribbled to the home 25,where Foulkes was lucky in getting the ball and putting into touch. A series of scrimmages on the home lines fol- lowed, and Warrington looked likely for scoring when the St. Helens forwards succeeded in dribbling away. Heesom, however, sent the ball back in good style, and Warrington again tried hard to score but could not suc- ceed, the home forwards again getting the ball out of danger. From a line out. Burton secured and gave to Cross, who, alter a run, gave to Barn. who was only , brought down by Foulkes on the line. The visitors con- tinued to attack, the forwards playing a very strong game. Finally Sudlow relieved, and St. Helens took the ball to the Warrington 25. From a scrimmage,Ewan , picked up and gave to Sudlow who though smartly tackled by Barber, scored at the corner. Ewan took the place kick, but failed to improve the point. Half time arrived shortly afterwards with the play again in St. Helens ground. After the way they had played,it seemed certain that Warrington, with the wind at, their backs,would pile on a respectable score in the secand half, but St. Helens played a cautious game. Content with having scored, they played on the defensive, and though Warrington played up grandly they were unable to penetrate the admirable defence of the home backs, and an excellent and enjoyable game ended in a win for the home team by one try to nil.

div.head: RUNCORN v. TYLUESLEY.
div.p: RUNCORN v. TYLUESLEY.

Runcorn first team travelled to the colliery district on I Saturday. Although the team arrived soon after two o'clock, it was nearly four o'clock before the home team were ready to start. Both sides had no excuses regard- ing their teams, each club being well represented. Reece and Taylor made their first appearance for Runcorn this season. Faulkner was fortunate in. winning the toss,and elected to play with the wind, which blew strongly from goal to goal. Getting soon to work, a bout of passing, started by Abrams and handled by several backs, Dun- bavin raced along the touch line, and looked all over a scorer, but Trow getting up his opponent well iato touch, some very sharp scrimmages ensued, Berry clearing the danger by kicking in touch well down the ground. 'the Berrys gave Lawton a chance which was cut short by effective tackling, and by a general forward rash play again located in the home half. Tyldesley had several free kicks allowed, but they did not assist then% much, the ball being well returned, and invari- ably going dead beyond the goal line. At one time Faulkner raised the hopes of a really fine run down the c-ntre, and throwing to Myers, the position was im- proved, but the next pass being spoiled, a grand chance to score was allowed to slip. The position maintainedl was kept, and for some time the two Berrys had a fair amount of collaring to do to keep the Runcorn halves from dodging through. Half time arrived with no score. Tyldesley now had the aid of the wind, and their supporters expected great things. As the match proceedod, the Runcorn men played a most determined game, and keeping the ball loose, swarmed round their opponents. The Berrvs took on some passing, which being badly done lost them ground,as Robinson closed on Shaw, the result being that that player threw the ball wildly away. and Walker took near to the goal line, Trow being smart to stop what appeared a certain try. Some hard fought packs followed, and Buff Berry break- ing the rules, Runcorn claimed a free Ir,ck. Dunbavin making no mistake with his kick, a capital goal re- sulted. This gave Runcorn the lead. Getting to work aiain Tyldesley forwards made a strong effort, and hovering near the Runcorn goal,Berry claimed a penalty kick, and Shaw taking it sent the ball wide of the posts. As the game finished the home side played very wildly, missing several opportunities to improve their position. Final results :—Runcorn, three points ; Tyldesley nothing.

div.head: WIDNES v. LIVERSEDCE.
div.p: WIDNES v. LIVERSEDCE.

IThe opening of the new ground at Widnes on Satur- day, was the occasion for the mustering of 4,000 spectators. The team to try conclusions with Widnes was Liversedge,and long before their arrival the streets were crowded, especially at the Hallway Hotel, where Gossage's Band and the Subscription Band dis- coursed music. A number of streamers were extended from the hotel to the adjoining houses, and the road to the field was well filled with people. Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., C.C., kicked off amid applause. Play was quick, and by rapid paesing the visitors gained ground. Three minutes from the start Liversedge secured a try. The venue was then changed, and Widnes had a look in. Fearnley got the ball from a free kick, and his punt was smartly captured by Emery, by whose aid play was taken into the visitors' quarters. Widnes was quick on the ball, and good passing by the forwards resulted in Clarke securing a try,which Barber fructified amid great cheering. Play continued in favour of Widnes for some time, at the end of which a scrimmage took place near the home goal. The defence was,however,very stubborn, and the visitors' efforts to score were neutralised. A determined attempt to gain something tangible was almost successful, but Brennan was on the qui Live, and he punted the ball to safer quarters. Sharpe executed a brilliant rumpassing several of his opponents. He threw to Jenkinson, but that pie yer was neatly callared by Rispan,vvho was himself robbed. Liversedge again locked dangerous, but Brennan was to the fore with a powerful punt, and the Widnes men took up the attack. They had hard lines on touch, and Barber got in some good work, but Fearnley was a tower of strength at back, and was instrumental in saving, some extremely dangerous attacks. Ead to end play supervened, after which Widnes initiated a move, and hostilities were transferred again to the visi- tors' twenty-five. Rispan and Johnson were conspicuous in this portion of the game, and.the spectators showed 1 theirappr.niation of the tactics by heartily applauding them. Play continued of a fast and interesting nature, ' and half time arrived with the score Whines one goal, Liversedge one try. In the second half the visitors had the best of matters. Barber started for Whines, who were the first to attack. They were, however, repelled, and the visitors took up the running. Wood and Sharp created cheers by a good run on the wing, and a minute later Womerslev secured a try, which was not improved upon. Matters looked bad for Widnes, who were con- fined for s‘me time within their 25. Brennan tackled flu the line, but the ball went into touch. Sharp, got in hi fine style, but his attempt was nentralized by a piece of good play by Brennan. Again Widnes took up the runn- inf.:, but Fearnley relieved the pressure with a big punt, the ball ultimately going into touch. Play became of a somewhat desultory nature. On several oecasions the Widnes lines were with difficulty kept intact. Nevitt and Archer proved barriers in the way of approach,and after the leather had been kept dangerously near the I home goal, temporary relief was effected. Barber ini- tiated a run,and Johnson and Derbyshire sprinted away. 1 Their progress, howevers was short, Thornton and Wood intercepting. The latter kicked forward, and from a

div.head: LANCASHIRE v. CHESHIRE.
div.p: LANCASHIRE v. CHESHIRE.

The Lancashire and Cheshire representatives on the committee of the Northern Union met at the Spread Eagle Hotel, Manftester, last evening, to select the teams for the Lancashire v. Cheshire match to be played at Stockport next Monday. The players selected were as follows :—Lancashire : J. Winstanley (Wigan) „ back ; F. Barber (Warrington), S. Lees (Oldham), H. Chap- man (Broughton Rangers), and J. Hurst (Oldham), three-quarter backs; H. Varley (Oldham, captain) and A. Lees (Oldham), hail backs ; W. Unsworth (Wigan), E. Bonser (Oldham), W. Nevins (Warrington), J. Worth- ington (Tyldesley), T. Smith (Leigh), W. Briers (St. Helens), J. Brown (Wigan),and W. Roberts (Tyldesley), forwards. Reserves: T. Coop (Leigh), back ; J. P. Taylor (Oldham) and 0. fdidgeley (Rochdale Hornets), centre three-quarters ; R. Doherty (St. Helens) and J. Lawton (Tyldesley), wingthree-cpiarters ; J. Mullineux (Leigh), half back ;.J. Johnson (Widnes), A. Hill (Roch- dale Hornets),and P. Taylor (Leigh),forwards. Cheshire : F. Saville (Stockport), full back ; r. Warder (Runcorn), G. Robinson (R4ncorn), J. Wersley, and W. Bailey (Stockport), three-quarter backs ; S. Abrams and J. Faulkner (Runcorn), half backs ; W. Faulkner, A. Taylor, EL Farmer, and J. Langley (Runcorn), J. Mottershead, R. Morton, T. Gibson, and C. Wrigley (Stockport), forwards. Reserves: J. Jolley (Runcorn), lull back El. Mayers (Runcorn), three-quarter back ; J. Norris (Stockport), half back ; S. Johnson (Runcorn), and R. Roberts (Stockport), forwards.

RTJHOORN RECRELTION v. CHESTER COLLEGE.—Hayed at Chesterpn Saturday. The Collegians had the wind in , their favour during the first half of the game. The game was evenly contested at the onset, but the Recreation men soon warmed to their work, and called upon the homesters to defend. The passirg and running of the Runcorn men was far superior to that of their opponents and as a result Worrall scored two tries, and Hopley, Melia and Sutton one each. At half-time the score stood, Runcorn Recreation one goal,four tries; Chester College, nil. On re-starting:the Collegians put on a better front, being aided by playing down hill. The combination of the Runcorn men was, however, more pr‘mounced. The forwards naanceuvred the scrimmages in good style, and enabled the backs to pass to each other neatly. Several more tries were scored by the vii-itors, Whitney convert- ing two of them into goals. The final result read : Runcorn Recreation, 3 goals, 6 tries, 4 minors ; Chester College, nil.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

OI7GIITRINGTON PARK V. WARRINGTON RESERVE.—This match was played on the ground of the former at Float- ley, in a strong wind. The game was of a scrambling character throughout. The teams were evenly matched, good play being out of the question owing to the strong wind. In the end the home team retired defeated by a goal to nothing. • •

HOLY TRINITY V. WARRINGTON STAR.—This match was played on the Holy Trinity grouud on Saturday. The homesters won the toss, and elected to play against a strong breeze. The Star kicked off and made a rush to the home goal and scored in the first few minutes. The ball being again set in motion a rough and tumble game ensued. Each goal was well attacked, the homesters missing several good openings, while the Star put two more goals to their credit, and at half time the score read three goals to nil. During the second half the Trinitarians played their opponents almost to a stand- still, and were entirely 'on the aggressive. Three goals were quickly placed to their credit, and the match ulti- mately ended in a draw of three goals each.

WLR RINOTON V. LIVERPOOL CASUALS.—The return fixture was decided on the Arpley enclosure on Saturday. Jardine put the ball in motion for the Casuals, who were quickly in evidence in front of Webster, who cleared nicely. Temporary relief came with the ball going over the line. Selby got away from the kick out, and made good progress with a dodgy run, but found Hughes just a point too good, and a moment later the sphere was , again over the Warrington line. The Liverpool men were once more on the aggressive, and Webster was called upon to defend his charge. Marshall assisted in the clearance, and from his kick Connor was just get- ting into his stride when he was fouled. Warrington now had a spell of attack, Selby and Jewkes putting in some good work, a grand shot by the former deserving a better fate. The game was being evenly contested until an appeal for hands against Warrington gave the visitors another opportunity of visiting the local custodian, Jardine putting the finishing touch to a good bit of work to the evident surprise of Webster, who had miscalcul- ated the shot. J. Mather fell back into his accustomed position at full back, Broughall going half back. gelby and T. Mather got nicely away, the latter's shot being cleared. The Liverpool front division now made racks for Warrington territory, but had the worst of an argu- ment with J. Mather, who put Selby in possession, that player making a good dodgy run, but was in torn stopped by Woodruffe. The whistle blew for half time shortly afterwards with Hughes in possession and the score—Liverpool, one; Warrington, none. Play in the second half was very interesting, the final scores reading —Casuals, two goals; Warrington, two goals.

PENKETH SCHOOL v. STOCKTON HEATH RESERVE.— These teams met at Stockton Heath on Saturday with a cross wind blowing, which made acPurate play very difficult. 'F lie school playing down hill carried the ball directly to their.opprnente goal, and the custodian was kept very busy for the first quarter of an hour,Reynolds, Lloyd and Harlow each trying at goal, without success. A corner for the school was headed out, but Andrew put in a neat shot from the half back and notched the first point for the school. The home team tried hard to score but several times failed at the last moment and Marrow saved some good shots. After half time Reynolds put in several fast runs for the school, but the home custodian was equal to the occasion, keeping the ball out in splen- did style. At the last a scrimmage in goal resulted in a second point for the school from the foot of the opposing back. This was quickly followed by a third from Rey- holds. After a futile shot the school forwards secured the ball from the kick off and passing with great judg- ment on the right wing, worked the ball in without their opponents touching it at all, and Harlow got the fourth point. The feature ef the game was Pollard's play at centre half, while Lloyd at the right wing centred very well considering the very strong wind. Score . School, four ; Stockton Heath, nil.

STOCKTON BEATH V. WALKER'S BREWERY.—PIayed on the Brewery ground on Saturday, in quite a gale of wind. The homesters, winning the toss, took advan- , tags of the elements, and from the kick-off took the ball well down the field, but the visitors' backs were safe and the leather was returned to half way. The Stockton Heath forwards then got away, and Webb scored the first goal. From the restart the Brewery front rank rushed down the field, and ilartley sent in a shot which hit the crossbar, and went through, thus equalizing. The visitors not to be denied, went away with a dash, and Podmore shot through, but the referee disallowed what was apparently a fair goal.Eyen play followed;and half-time arrived l with the score—Brewery, one; Stock- ton Heath, one. On resuming, it was soon apparent that the Heathens held the upper liand,as the homestera only once crossed the half-way line. Goals were scored by Webb, Johnson, and Probert, and the score would have been much larger but for the poor shooting of the visiting forwards. At the call of time Stockton fieath an out winners by four goals to ene.
