div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

Warrington lost twu more points on Saturday, but it is only fair to say that they wete by no means disgraced. A solitary try separated St. Helens and themselves,at the end of the game, which was decidedly hard lines as they were quite equal to their opponents. The re-organised team are " on the improve" undoubtedly, and I venture to predict before the season is finished,several teams will know it. They have been at a disadvantage so far owing to the fact that out of four games they have played, only one was at home, and that they won easily. They have done by no means badly, especially on Satur- day, for not many teams return home victorious from St. Helens.

We shall see them to-day for the first t;ml at home for a Saturday match, and Wakefield Trinity will be a very attractive" bill of fare." The Trinity have for the past few years lost a great deal of their fame in the football world, but still they can spring surprises even yet. Last year after a most disastrous series of defeats, they sud- denly came out in the Yorkshire Cup ties, and defeated several of the crack Yorkshire teams in the most decisive fashion. This year, they have retained their character, for though they have done worse than Warrington, in the Northern League, they were the first to put a spoke in Wigan's progress, and although up to the time of meeting them, Wigan had not a point scored against them, Wakefield put on no fewer than 16 points. Last Saturday, they beat Leeds by two tries to a try. They have, however,not yet been victorious away from home, and Warrington is not likely to be the place where their ill-luck in this respect will be broken.

Wakefield Trinity have been several times previously to Warrington, but it was only on the last occasion that Warrington beat them, by a dropped goal which Jolley kicked from the middle of his opponents, a minutebefore the end of the game. Jolley on that occasion was carried shoulder high off the field. There is not a single player, unless it is Nevins, now left of the team which beat Wakefield, owing to the numerous changes which has been made of late. The following is the team selected to do service for Warrington: Heesom,full back; Barber, Cross, Burton and Broady, three-quarters ; Nevins and Floughton, half backs ; Burrows, Barrett, Saunders, Hill, Thornton, Fairhurst, Wilcock and Andrews, forwards.

At the match with St. Helens on Saturday, the for- wards played a strong game, and the halves were pretty evenly matched. At three quarters, the Warrington quartette were in brilliant form, especially Barber and Burton. Barber had the hardest of luck on one occasion especially when he was tackled just as he got to the line. Up to the present, both he and Burton have had hard lines as on many occasions they have all but scored. Heesom was every whit the equal of Foulkes, who repre- sented Lancashire county last season, and Warring zoo have no fear of this department of the team now.

I am glad to notice that two Warrington men have ob- tained county honours in the coming match between Lancashire and Cheshire. Barber is without doubt, one of the most brilliant wings in the county and no surprise can be expressed that he is one of the chosen three-quar- ters. Although he has only played in first class football for three years he will have the distinction of having played both for Lancashire and Cheshire. Not many football players of many years standing can boast of the honour of representing two counties.

The other Warrington player chosen to represent his county is" Bill" Nevins. Although Nevins at present plays half back, he will be a forward in the county match. Like Barber he has been a county man before,and it waster Lancashire against Cheshire on that occasion. The selection of Nevins will give great pleasure to War- rington footballers,for if there is a man in the team who deserves the honour, it is he. It would be almost im- possible to find a more hard working player anywhere. Wherever the ball is. Nevins is not far away. He can also adapt himself to any position. Full back, three quarters, half back, or forward are all alike to him. In tact, in one match last season he took every position at various times with the exception of full back.

There was a number of very narrow victories among Northern Union clubs on Saturday. In six out of the eleven matches played, only three points separated the winning from the lwates teams. These were Halifax and Hunslet, St. Helens and Warrington, Brighouse Rangers and Manningham, Wakefield Trinity and Leeds, Rochdale Hornets and Broughton Rangers, Runcorn and Tyldesley. The teams were evidently well balanced,and to add to these, Wigan and Bradford played a pointless draw. Wigan by going to Brighouse on Monday and playing a draw again, have become the champion draw- ists of the League. It is too early to talk with any con- fidence about the championship, for with such results as those chronicled above, it would be a wise man who could have any idea of the final result of the competi- tion.

Leigh are at any rate going strong and are only a point behind the leaders—Bradford, and have a match in hand. They settled Batley for the time being by eight points to nil, and now, with Halifax, are the only team who have lost no more than two points on the league table. They are exceptionly strong forward,!and it is here that they have won their victories.

Rochdale Hornets are improving to judge from their play during the past week. Previous to Monday of last week, they had not scored a solitary point, but now they have three, and in the Lancashire and Cheshire section, they have actually four clubs below them. Broughton Rangers who fell victims to them on Saturday, are on the other hand going worse, and in the League they tie with Rochdale Hornets for the bottom place. Oldham have now got into their stride, and Hull were made to it with a vengeance They have,however,one defect know in their team which thy always have had, and that is the want of a goal kicker. They scored five tries on Saturday, some in easy positions, but not one was con- verted into a goal. This is a serious matter now that there is a championship competition, for the position of a club may be decided by the score average, and then a few goals would be very useful.

IS IT DESIRABLE TO BE GREAT?

PECULIARITIES OF MEN OF GENIUS. Someone has, says a writer in the "Newcastle Weekly Chronicle," wisely observed that every evil that mili- tates against a man's happiness is in each case more or less counteracted by some form of compensation, or, in other words, whenever nature has richly endowed an individual in one direction she has accompanied it by some detrimental attribute. It is especially so in the case of the psychical function, or intellectuality: hence it has been asserted that genius is an abnormality—a sign of insanity. Eminent modern writers and scientists have lately dwelt upon the association of genius and insanity in a way to imply an original discovery of to-day ; but they are strangely mistaken, for we find the subject more than vaguely recognised in the records of the long past. For instance, the prophets cf old were looked upon by the masses as men with a mental kink; in proof, we have only to call to mind the origin or literal meaning of the word " prophet." And in our day the modern pro- phet is regarded by most persons as a mild and harm- less lunatic, though the weather-Prophet is scarcely regarded as altogether harmless—" at times and in places*" We do not need to ransack ancient books that are inaccessible to the many, for evidence to show that genius was long ago considered to be in some way allied to madness ; for many notable examples of this belief exist in the Bible, Perhaps one of the most convincing is the explanation of Festus--" Paul, much learning bath made thee mad "—a philosophic and realistic utterance that is to this day often applied to genius. We will presently return to other Biblical references ; but before doing so we would like to draw attention to an original observation that we found in amonograph by Dr. James Weir some twelve months ago. We have kept the new light in view ever since, and reflection convinces us that Dr. Weir's observation is original, true and most inter- esting. He says: "It is a strange fact, and one not noticed by Lornbroso, or auy other writer as far as I know, that mechanical geniuses, or those who for the most part deal with material facts, do not, as a rule, show any signs of degeneration.' I have only to instance Darwin, Galileo, Edison, Watts, Rumsey, Howe, and Morse, to prove the truth of this assertion. It is only the genius of eestheticism, the genius of the emotions, that is generally.accompanied'by unmistakable signs of degeneration." The list of names might have been con- siderably extended, and might have included some of local men of mechanical genius, such as Armstrong, George Stephenson. Sze. To return to Bible history for further proof of the kinship of genius and insanity (a part of the subject that is also dealt with in an interesting manner in the monograph referred to), we learn that Saul, the first King of Israel, was a man of genius, amd at times a, madman. We read that before his coronation he was seized with an attack of madness and joined a company of kindred eccentrics. His friends and acquaintances were naturally surprised, and exclaimed : " Is Saul among the prophets ?" i.e.," Has Saul become insane ?" Agaia, we are told that he was suddenly seized with an attack of; homicidal impulse and tried to kill David. Be- fore this time he had repeated attacks ef enadness which only the harp of David could control ad subdue. David himself was a man whose mental eq ,ffibrium was not well established, as his history cies y indicates. He forsook his God, indulged in licent ;Jura practices, and was, withal, a very immoral man at times. Whilst recognising the greatness of many of the Hebrew propkets,iG is painful to acknowledge how eccentric and immoral a great number of them were. The mighty Jeremiah journeyed to the river Euphrates to hide a linen girdle ; Hosea married a woman of ill-fame ; Isaiah walked in view of his people divested of all clothing •, Ezekiel imagined that he must dig a hole in the wall of his house to get out his household goods, instead of us- ing the ordinary door ; and, lastly, the Song of Solo- mon shows undoubted evidence of a sensually disordered brain. Is it desirable to be great? Well, suicide is often the melancholy end of greatness. The list of names of the men of genius who have terminated their own exist- ences is too long to detail, and ettends from David to, say, Chatterton, " the marvellous boy, the sleepless soul that perished in his pride." Then, again, St. Vitas's dance has often made sad havoc with the overetrung nerves of the man of genius. Such was the case with Socrates, Napoleon, Dr. Jcbnson, Thomas Campbell,and a host ef others. •To be truly great is often to be very poor. Poverty seems to be a characteristic of genius. The following among others lived in attics, and some died there :—Addison, Chatterton, Goldsmith, Hayden, Faraday, De Quincey, Dr. Johnson, Dickens in youth, Hans Andersen, Collins, Benjamin Franklin, Burns, Hogarth, and Watts. And, alas ! many great men have had to sooth their nerves with morphia er opium, or call upon alcohol to counteract temporary fits of physical or mental depres- sion ; and how often we have to lament that the great and clever man of our acquaintance is a drunkard, and to regret that mingled with the history of many of the great minds that have in the past stimulated the ad- vance of civilization comes also the painful record of their indulgence in alcohol or opium I Would that we could draw an impenetrable veil that would shut out their degradation ! But history should be impartial ; otherwise its lessons would be misleading. Thus Lom- broso tells us that " Alexandra died after having ten times emptied the goblet of Hercules, and that it was without doubt in an alcoholic attack, whilst pursuing naked the infamous Thais—that he killed his dearest friend. Caesar was often carried home on the shoulders of kis soldiers. Neither Socrates nor Seneca, nor Alcibiades,nor Cato,nor Peter the Great (nor his wife Catherine, nor his daughter Elizabeth) were remarkable for their abstinence. Tiberius Nero was called by the Roman soldiers Biberius Mero. Septimus Severus and Mehemet 11. succumbed to drunkenness or delirium tremens." It was opium or alcohol with Charles Lamb, Handel, Coleridge, Thomp- son, Addison, Steele, Alfred de Musset,Morland,Hartley, Turner, Gluck, Tasso, and a host of others. Some have been so void of self-control as to die in jail for offences against morality or as common felons. Many men of mark have been the victims of epilepsy—a nervous malady. The list of such names is a long one. But the mention of epilepsy, so often the curse of the men who have dazzled the intellectual world, brings to remembr- ance the fact that the Church which was for centuries at the head of that world took ages to recognise epilepsy as a disease. When a man was seized with a convul- sion attack of this malady, he was considered to be " born of the devil," and for long exorcism was re- garded as one of the great accomplishments and privi- leges of ecclesiastics. To doubt that this manifestation of disease was the work of the devil was to embrace , Atheism; and to say anything disparagingly of the Church's method of exorcism was both disrespectful to that institution and dangerous to the soul. The ritual of exorcism was elaborate and at the same time comi- cal. To begin with an endeavour was made to compel " the devil "to quit under a fueilade of vulgar abuse— he was called " a sooty spirit." " a lean sow," "a mangy beast," and other expressions were used that weuld not lee considered polite in our day. We have heated how a woman who was wonderfully skilled in vituperative language was reduced to tears and then silence on being addressed as an isosceles triangle and a parallelogram ; so on a .similar principle the officiating clergyman endeavoured to cast out the evil spirit. be calling him athanatora, tetragammaton' or schem- hamphora. If still obdurate—that is, if the epilepic fit Still continued—nauseous drugs were burnt under the victim's nose ; failing this:remedy, the devil was coaxed by the apocalyse and the golden candle-sticks. At this point the patience of the priest usually broke down, and he took to cursing the devil in a manner that no doubt suggested the legend of the Jackdaw of Rheims, and often with no other result than " nobody was one penny the worse." All this is comical, but the painful part of the process is yet to be referred to—scourging and torture—which were freely practised to the ever- lasting reproach of the Church as then existent. To resume: We cannot escape from the conviction that great men and women, if not exactly insane, are frequently eccentric, melancholic or excitable—subject, that is, to various forms of nervous diseases. Many are drunkards or opium-eaters, and some grossly immoral: and, curiously the msthetical individual, with a high development of the faculy of taste, has often presented to the world shocking instances of immorality. The peculiarities of greatness, and they are many, are called into action or are accentuated by varinus agents—it may be wearing enthusiasm, the monotonous pursuit of one or more subjects, isolation, Ztc., all rubbed in by the misery and disappointments that flow from the neglect and indifference of an unappreciative world. Of course, much of the trouble that occasionally overtakes the man of eminence is sought by himself let us remind the man of genius and the man of talent (very different qualities) that the chance of long life and lasting fame depend largely upon the common-sense observance of the ' laws that govern the physical or mental health. But there are often agencies at work that are beyond the control of the genius, and so irrevocably so that it seems ietermined by nature that, though each great mind , gives in turn an impulse to civilization, yet it is at the cost of the individual born to greatness.

THE MIIRDEit OF MR. STOKES..
STARTLING REVELATIONS.

A correspondent of the " Pall Mall Gazette" has had and interview with: Dr. Michaux, who was the only European witness of the trial an condemnation of Mr. Stokes by Captain Lothaire. Stokes, it appears, came into the camp unaccompanied by any one except his per- sonal servants, and immediately on his arrival was in- formed by Lothaire (through Dr. Michaux, who acted as interpreter, the officer not understanding English) that he would be charged witn having sold guns and powder to the Arabs. Next morning he was brought before Lothaire, whp " alone tried him, judged him, and sen- tenced him." Dr. Michaux merely acted as interpreter. No other white man, I repeat, was in camp. I prefer , not to express an opinion. All I can say is that beyond acting as interpreter, I had nothing to do with the trial. " Can you tell me whether any witnesses were called ?" "Yes, a few Arabs, among them men who had in their possession Sniders and Mausers which they stated they had purchased from Stokes." How long did the trial last ?" Between one and two hours." " And the evid- ence over, what took place ?" "Lothaire said to Stokes, to whom I translated it, that he was sentenced to death . and would be executed the following day. Stokes was so dumbfounded that he could find nothing to say and retired to his hut. He sent for me there and implored me to intercede for him with Lothaire. I had already done so without success, and again I made the attempt. I employed every argument I could think of. I suggested Stokes should be sent to Boma, the capital of the Congo State, but Lothaire turned a deaf ear to all my interces- sions. AS a last resource I begged for a reprieve for a few days during which time fresh evidence might be pro- cured. But this was equally refused. I then thought of looking through the code, in order to find out whether Lothaire really had power to inflict the punishment of death on Stokes, but I had no copy with me, and having asked Lothaire for one I found that he equally possessed none. I was tlaeretore unable to find out what his powers really were " " What did Stokes do ? " I continued, "after his con- viction ? Did he write or make his will, or asked to be allowed to do so F" No, he was so much upset, as you may well imagine, that he remained in a state of semi- collapse. He asked for nothing, and wrote nothing ; he only begged me, as I said before, to intercede for him. His will, however, was already drawn up,and was found among the papers subsequently sent down by Lieuten- ant Henri. In it, a provision, I believe, was made for his black children. A yearly income is to be paid to them through an English missionary, near some lake (sic). I had already begged Lothaire several times dur- ing the day not to carry out Stoke's sentence at once. When night camel made one more appeal to Lothaire, but in vain. I thought I would try again the next day, I but at five in the morning my servant came to call me, , and in an excited tone said, • Master, the white man is dead ! ' Tula gave me a terrible shock. I got up hur- riedly and found that the gallows had been erected, at , the toot of which was a newly-made grave. In it rested Stokes, who had just been executed, and who was im- mediately afterwards buried. This while I was asleep. Lothaire subseqaently told me that Stokes was sleeping , when he was fetched to be led to his death." ' The" Pall Mall Gazette," commenting en the revela- tions summarized above, remarks ;—ln order to relieve himself of Dr. Michaux's anneals and pretests Lothaire hung his prisoner in the early dawn. There is noth- ing to show that he was dead when they buried him at the foot of the ganows, or to prove that he was not tor- tured before execution. The story, as set forth above, is that of as black a crime as was ever exposed, and if Mr. Stokes is not signally avenged the lives of white men in South Africa will be at the mercey of every law- less ruffian who happens to wear a uniform.

HOME RULE AND HENRY GRATTAN. Sir,—ln my concluding sentence in last week's issue, I Said, " It may be confidently asserted that there is no fragment of literature in the English language which within the same small compass deals so completely and powerfully with the subject, e.g. Grattan's celebrated sketch el the Earl of Chatham." It is difficult,however, to quote where the whole is so short, and where every nascence is a masterpiece, out the description of Chat- ham's oratory, combining, as it does, melodious and xnajestic language with great and striking ideas, may be Singled out far notice. "His eloquence was an era in the senate, peculiar and Spontaneous; familiarly expres- sing gigantic sentiments and expressive wisdom ; not like the torrent of Demosthenes or the splendid confla- gration of Tully,it resembles sometimes the thunder and sometimes the music of the spheres. Like Murray, he did not conduct the understanding through the painful Sublety of argumentation ; nor was he, like Townshend, for ever on the rack of exertion ; but rather lightened Upon the subject,and reached the points by the flashings of his mind, which, like those of his eye, were felt, but Could not be followed." In the House of Commons Grattan heard his illustri- ous countryman, Burke, for whom he at once formed a very high admiration. "Burke," hc writes to a friend in Ireland, "the only orator I have yet met or heard, in the House of Commons here (and his character arises from this matter, not his delivery), was ingenious, ora- Unica', not undaunted." In another letter he says: "Burke is unquestionably the first orator among the Commons of England; boundless in knowledge, instan- taneous in his apprehensions aid abundant and forcible in his language ;he speaks with prDfound attention and acknowledged superiority, notwithstanding the want of energy, the want of grace, the want of elegance in his manner." Grattan was himself a born orator; he had instinctive liking for public speaking, and it may be 4magined that the effect upon him when he was young and impressionable,of hearing these great masters of the art was to stimulate and excite him in the direction in which he was naturally bent. So, during the time he was at London, his mind was continually occupied with the subject, and he indulged in the practice of m iking speeches when he was alone to such an exteat that his landlady thought he was mad. "The gentle- man," she said," used to walk up and down the garden most of the night, speaking to himself; and, though alone, be was continually addressing someone by the, name of Mr. Speaker; that it was not possible he could be in his senses," and she begged they would take him away, and that if they did she would forgive him all the tent that was due. Be went to live at Windsor Forest, and spent whole moonlight nights in rambling in the thickets and plantations. He would sometimes pause and address a tree in soliloquy, and on one occasion he stopped at a gibbet and commencsd apostrophising the chains in an animated strain, when he suddenly felt a tap on his shoulder, and on turning round was accosted by a stranger, " How the devil did you get down ?" To which Grattan replied, "Sir, I suppose you have an aterest in that qaestion." At this time Henry Grattan also indulged a great deal in private theatricals. He took part in them along with Mr. Flood, Mr. Bushe. and Mr. (afterwards Sir Hercules) Laagrishe. He also took pains to learn what was very necessary for an Irish gentleman of those days—to aim accurately with the pistol, an accomplishment which he found very useful in !-ter years.—Yours truly,
J. KILGALLON.

ROM ANES IN LITTLE; BALFOUR AT LARGE. "Whose fouudation is in the dust." Job. iv. 19. Sir,—A private, and I presume confidential, com- munication now before me, advises me to "read Romanes, who from being a rejector of theism became a believing Christian." "Go to," saith the writer, " study him and do likewise." -- Excellent advise, though Coming rather late,as I had studied Romanes' " thoughts on religion "long ere receiving 'this advice, so piously and gratuitously tendered. Romans professes to approach the subject from a philosophical rather than a theologi- cal position. As a philosopher then I had read his work, with that awe and reverenca due from a common per- son endowed only with comrson sense to one so immeas- urably his superior—as a mere mortal might listen to an olympian voice. Hear, then, what the ",deep philosophic rage " has to say about " Adam, the Fall, the Origin of Evil." " These all taken together as Christian dogmas, are undoubtedly hard hit by the scientific proof of evolution (but are the only dogmas which can fairly be said to be so), and, as con- stitutency the logical basis of the whole plan they do appear at first sight necessarily to involve in their dis- truction that of the entire superstructure. But the ques- tion is whether they have been destroyed for a pure agnostic. In other words,whether my principles are not as applicable in turning the flank of infidelity hose, as everywhere else. Firt, as regards Adam and Eve, ob- serve, to begin with, that long before Darwin the story of man in Paradise was recogniset by thoughtful theo- logians as allegorical. " Then he goes on to brand" this Story "as a poem as distinguished from history "!! Quite unhistorical says the philosopher. That is—a fable—not true—says commonsense. And, adds the common, unphilosophical person, if the foundation of popular Christianity be a myth or fable and untrue, the popular faith must indeed be "hard hit" and be existing only by the general ignorance of these facts. But this is only what common people, with only commonsense to guide them, might think, and shows the advantage of philo- sophising and getting so much above common folk as to bave your head in the clouds. If you have" principles" which must be made "applicable to turning the flank of Mfidelity " the destruction of the formation need not impair the stability of the superstructure. It is, to such, a mere matter of detail that Adam was a myth and Eve an allegory. And Commonsense turns round and asks "Where then does the impregnability of the "Impreg- nable Rock begin ? " Balfour's " Foundations of Belief" rest upon the same basis and are equally undermined by the current commonsense. The man who can read the concluding verses of Luke iii., 23 as poetry, must indeed, have philosophised himself into a very superior being. In conclusion, I should say, that commonseese must now regard this " allegory " and the superatrueture of modern mythology founded upon it much as the Grec- ian mythology Gf the time of Socrates was regarded,i.e.,' as a matter of amusement to the learned and irrational belief to the crowd. But,though founded upon a fable-- nrhistorical—and tottning to its fall, the popular faith br - vasted interests and "like the creaking gate hangs emolumental Lo its teachers and a delusive diver- sion to the taught. But,again,this is only what common-, voile thinks which has net its head in the clouds.— Trely yours,

div.head: JOHN PEERS.
div.p: JOHN PEERS.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT. A special meeting of the members of the Runcorn School Board was held on Tuesday in the Board room at the Town Hall, Runcorn. :Dar. J.i'ritchard occupied the chair. and there were also present : Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall. Mr. E. Imison,J.P.,and Mr. Moss (clerk). The business of the Board was to receive the annual statement of the receipts and expenditure for the year ending September 29th, 1895. The statement showed- that the balance on September 29th, 1894 was £543 144. 4d.; the grants from the Education Department and Science and Art Department were £1,531 104. 6d.; under the Technical Instruction Act, 1889, £217 14s. ; school fees, £33 15a. 21.; sales of books to children,£2l 19.11 d., from the rating authorities (being an equivalent to a rate of sd. in the £ on £60•815), £1,300 ; other receipts in- cluding £l7 16s. 6d. contributions from parents towards maintenance of blind and deaf children,£29 165.;making a total of £3,677 11s. 11d. The expenditure included salaries of officers of the Board, £3OO 16s. ; legal and other expenses of administration, £BB 194. 3.1.; salaries and remuneration of teachers. £1.267 lie. 21. ; books, apparatus and stationery, £lOl 4.6. Td.; fuel light, clean- replacement of furniture, and repairs to buildings and furniture, £166 10s. 4d. ; rents, rates, taxes, and insurance, £9 33. id. • other expenses, 14.. 4d.; contri- butions to Industrial' schools, £33 164. 2.1. ; expenses under the Technical Instruction Act, 1809. £220 24. 5!.: principal repaid on loans, £177 18s. 8 ; interest cn loans, £152 18i.; maintenance of blind and deaf children, £6B 16s. 6d.; balances on September 29th, 1895, £1,089 Is. 5d., total £3,677 lls. 11d. The Chairman in moving the adop',ion of the report said taking the statement as a whole they fund on com- paring it with the previous year that tlqire was an in- crease of expenditure of about £BO. £5O of this amount was owing to the cost of blind apt; dear children which I was a new responsibility the Hoard had had to incur. ' They had received from the rate £1,300. whieh was £3OO MVO than the previous year, and equivalent to a rate of ss. in the £, being a penny of an increase. They had bad to make a precept on the overseers to provide extra Capital consequent on the taking over of the Wesleyan schools. They had to provide monthly for an expendi- ture of from £9O to £lOO to pay teachers' calaries and other working expenses. The fee grant came in quarterly but the principal grant or examination grant only came in at the end of the year. The in- crease in that way had got to be provided in the form of working capital, but it would at the close of the year be largely recouped. Any party commancing a new schnol had to provide the working capital as the Board had to do in connection with Mill Brow and Greenway-road schools, consequent on the revenue com- ing in at the close of the school year. They hoped that the cost to the ratepayers at the end of the year would nor be considerable.-Dr. McDougall seconded the adcp- tion of the report.-The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi hoped that the rates would not be further increasicd.-The report was then adopted. This was all the public business. lured:

div.head: EARLE STO WN IND N EWTON.
div.p: EARLE STO WN IND N EWTON.
POLICE CHANGES AT EARLESTOWN.
In place of P.C. Grlen who has been transferred to TyWesley, P.C. Bullen has been stationed at Earlestown. P.C. Williamson has been transferred to West Derby vice P.C. Dickson, Newton.

div.head: EARLESTOWN ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY.
div.p: EARLESTOWN ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY.

At a meeting of the Earlestowu Orchestral So- ciety held on Wednesday night, the question of rendering aid to some local charity was discussed. Eventually it was resolved to devote the psoceeds of a concert to the Medical Aid Society's funds. It was thought desirable to enlist the services of local artistes, and thus make the concert a purely local affair. The concert is to take place in the Town Hall early in November.

div.head: EA.B.LESTOWN GOSPA MISSION.
div.p: EA.B.LESTOWN GOSPA MISSION.

At the Co-operative Hall,Earlestown, on Saturday Right, in connection with the above, a lecture entitled " Esther, the beautiful queen," was given before a fair attendance by Mrs. laylor of Manches- ter. The Rev. T. R. Matthews presided, and the lecture which was descriptive of the biblical char- acter was of an interesting character, and was intently listened to. On the following day,Sunday, the same lady conducted the services, which were in aid of the Mission funds. VULCAN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.

On SaturAay evening in the above schoolroom Mr. Hartley, of Manchester, gave a magic lantern entertainment in aid of the funds. There was a crowded audierce, and the subjects thrown on the sheet were " The story of poor Mike," " Eva's kiss," and' Little Flo," concluding with" A day in Lou- th-al," Mr. Hartley describing the views in a lucid and interesting manner. On Sunday the same gentleman conducted a lantern service, entitlod "Bible pictures and other lessons." The service was well attended, and special hymns were sung by the choir.

div.head: ST. JABS' CHURCH, HAYCOCK.
div.p: ST. JABS' CHURCH, HAYCOCK.

The annual harvest thanksgiving services in con- nection with the above church were held on Satur- day. The church was profusely but neatly decor- ated with fliwers, fruit, vegetables and cereals, the decorations hiving been carried out under the supervision of the churchwardens and sidemen. Special hymns and anthems were sung by the choir and the pulpit at the morning service was occu- pied by the Rev. F. W. Johnstone, curate of New- ton, and in the evening by the Rev. J. W. Barnes,of St. Michael's, Wigan. There were large congrega- tions, and the collections were in aid of the church debt.

div.head: 1.0.G.T
div.p: The usual weekly session of the Earlestown Ebenezer Lodge, No. 752, was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall on Tuesday evening. • The session was called to order at 8 p.m. by Bro. W. Hatton, C.T. The sick committee gave their report. Bro. T. Dean, secretary, was reported sick and the members tendered their sympathy to him in his illness. The members and friends afterwards sat down to a sub• stantial potato pie supper which was provided on an excellent scale by the following : Sisters 1 aylor, Woods,Hall,Brown and Hatton. The m3mbers and friends tendered the a a hearty vote of thanks for their excellent arrangements. The members and friends left at 9.30 having fully enjoyed themselves with the supper and also one or two Lancashire readings.

div.head: EARL ESTOWN WESLEYA N CHURCH.
div.p: EARL ESTOWN WESLEYA N CHURCH.

In connection with the above special harvest thanksgiving services were held in the church on Sunday. This is the first occasion on which such services have been held in the Wesleyan Church at Earlestown, and the venture was rather a nlvelty to the congregation. The communion table and pulpit were very nicely decorated with flower, fruit and vegaables, and the window recesses were also laden with the earth's products. Special anthems were sung by the choir at the morning and evening services, and solos were sung by Misses L. and M. Clare, Miss Eckersley, and Mr. F. P. Clare. The sermons were preached by the Rev. J. Bartley, resident minister, and the collections were in aid of the contingent fund.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARS.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARS.

The weekly se.sion of the Hope of Earlestown I Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall on Monday evening. Bro. J. Halton, C.T. presided, and there was a very large attendance of members and visitors. Five candidates were init- iated to membership. The report of the No.l Con- vention held at St. Helens on Saturday was read by Bro. C. Drew, and adopted. The arrangements for the holding of the 23rd anniversary of the lodge were completed. The programme for the evening was then proceeded with, Bro. J. T. Holli- day being responsible, when the following items were submitted : Piano sob, Bro. Willis ; recita- tion, " Welcome bonnie brid," Bro. W. Wilson ; song, "The old brigade," Bro. J. Hopkins ; reading, "Mother's prayer,' Bro. G. E. Warburton ; piano solo, Bro. Muscroft; Lancashire reading, Bro. G. Clarke. Br. J. Halton gave a brief address, and thanks to Bro. Holliday terminated the session,

div.head: YEOMANRY DINNER Al' NEWTON.
div.p: YEOMANRY DINNER Al' NEWTON.

The annual dinner given by Lord Newton to the " C "Troop (Newton) of the Lancashire Hussars, and tenants who provide horses for the troop took place on Saturday evening at the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton. About 85 sat down to an excellent repast prepared in goodly style by Mr. J. Dorman,and full justice was done to the edibles. The subsequent proceedings were presided over by Mr. F. Frost,who was supported at the cross table by Messrs. Stuart, G. Clarke, Hindley, Forster, Marsh, and Longton, the vice-chair being occupied by Sergeant Strange. Amongst the toasts proposed and honoured were " Lord Newton,"" Captain the lion. T. W. Leigh," " Mr. Pardey." Mr. Stewart in giving "The non- commissioned officers of the "C "troop," compli- mented the troop upon obtaining such an excellent report from the inspecting officer at Southport. Sergeant Strange responded on behalf of the troop. Songs were coniributed during the evening by Farrier Sergeant Ritchie, Corporal F_ wann, Sergeant Turner, Troopers Bush and Ritchie, and Ex-Tr3A e' Williams.

div.head: NEWTON NURSERY BOWLING CLUB.
div.p: NEWTON NURSERY BOWLING CLUB.

The annual closing handicap of this club was played on the home green on Saturday. The weather was all that could be desired and some good games were played. At the conclusion of the handicap the players adjourned to the White Lion Hotel, and after partaking of a substantial tea pro- vided by Mr. J. Chapmau, Councillor Simpson took charge of the subsequent proceedings. After a few appropriate remarks he proceeded to distribute the prizes, each player who bad taken part in the game receiving a prize of some kind. The first prizs, a copper kettle, was taken by T. Gorse ; second, copper kettle, F. Croston •, third, teapot, J. William- son ; fourth umbrella, J. Chapman ; fifth, umbrella, W. H. Ran all ; sixth, watch guard, J. J. Randall ; seventh, se, of carvers, W. McCormick; eighth, umbrella, J. Williamson ; ninth, umbrella, G. Mc Cormick ; tenth, set of carvers, R. Davies &c. The evening was afterwards spent in a convivial man- ner, songs being given by Messrs. F. Appleton, A' Boardman, W. Devereux, W. Kent, R. Knox, J. T. Randall, and others.

div.head: NO. 1 CONVENTION OF GOOD TEMPLAR&
div.p: NO. 1 CONVENTION OF GOOD TEMPLAR&

I The session of No;! Convention of South:West Lancashire was held at the Central Caf4, St. Helens, on Saturday. The Convention was opened by Bro. Quartermaster-Sergeant Roberts, of Warrington. The officers' reports were of an interesting nature, showing that they had been very active in getting the lodges throughout the year more earnest in the work of the order, and hopes of a general revival. There was a very large attendance of representa- tives and visitors present from Widnes, Wigan, Leigh,Earlestown, Warrington, Prescot,and Ashton. It was resolved " That the Convention tender their G.C.T. Bro. Malins their warmest thanks for the grand declaration of principle enunciated by him , with reference to the action of the Jlayor of Ches- . ter at the close of the late congress,in placing upon the table intoxicating liquors to welcome temper- ance delegates. Al-o tor his outspoken remarks upon Mr. Gladstone and the Gothenburg scheme,' enunciated by the Bishop of Chester, and pray that he may be long spared to carry on this noble war- fare." The resolution was signed on behalf of the Convention by C.C.T. C. Lee and C.E.S. Bro. Lindon. It was arranger' to hold the next Convention at Wesley Lodge, Warrington, which was in a low state, and it is hoped the visit will stir the order to more active work. A paper was then read by Bro. , Francis, written by Bro. Newell, " How to prepare good programmes for our lodge ses,ioos." A lengthy discussion followed, and thanks were tendered to the writer of the paper.the session aft, rwarils dos- ing. A public tea was afterward held followed by ' an entertainment over which Bro. J. W. Roberts I presided, supported by Bros. W. 11. Cook, D.C., and E. Newman, D.S.J.T. Addresses were given by the Chairman and Bro. Cook, it being Oa latter's first visit to the Convention. Songs, &c., were given, and an interesting gathering closed.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER l9, 1995.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, OCTOBER l9, 1995.
CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.

On Sunday last, sermons were preached in con- nection with the Diocesan Church of England Tem- perance Society, in the morning and afternoon it St. Peter's, Warrington, and in the evening at the Parish Church, Newtou-in-Makerfleld, by the Rev. J Hirst, Diocesan Secretary. The offertories were for the society's work. BAPTIST CHAPEL, BARLESTOWN.

On Thursday evening at the Baptist Chapel, Earlestown, the Rev, F. E. Miller, gave a lecture before a moderate audience, entitled " A holiday in Switzerland." The lecture was illustrated by means of the lime light, the lantern being manipulated by Mr. Lawson. It was very interesting and appeared to be much enjoyed by those present. BARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT BUILDING SOCIETY. The final meeting of the Directors preparatory to issuing the balance sheet for the past year's work- ing was held on Thursday night, when it was de- cided to declare a dividend of .5 per cent. and carry nearly .£lOO to tbe reserve fund. The society is at the present time in a sound financial position, and the .Jeclaration of a dividend of 5 per cent, will be received by the nr-mbers with satisfaction. The annual meeting AiII be held at the usual time.

persons in the audience took part, their subject being " mit ian Endeavour and the children." The Rev. JAMES Monona., of Derby, afterwards gave an address upon "Christian Endeavour and consecra- tion." He said that the great need of the Christian chursh to-day was consecration. He thought that the lite of a Christian should be spoilt in the service of Jesus Christ, and in personal devotion to Him. There were a great in.iny young men who had a really earnest desire to serve Christ and to devote their lives in His cause, but who thought that they could not be fully conse- crated. If they got face to face with Christ and put their lives and intellects under His control, there would be great results from that. They must yield the whole of their lives to Him, and then they would be safe- guarded wherever they went. Let them fully trust God, and they would gain the victory, and overc2me in every battle which they had to fight. 'I hey would have grace to resist temptation. They might be engaged ih business, and thsy must not shrink from letting their purpose be known. Mr. Mursell continued at length to give some sound advice to his hearers on the above su bjec:. Alter the singing of a hymn, tea was provided in the schoolroom over Arpley Station at which a good number sat down.

div.head: WARNING To CHILDREN.
div.p: A WARNING To CHILDREN.

On Tuesday afternoon when a lurry belonging to Bell and Co., Mineral Wieer Manufacturers, was passing along Crow Lane, a number of lads, just leaving the Catholic schools, ran behind and coin- irenced swinging on the back. It had not gone far before one of them, James Lacky, eight years of age, living in Legh-st., Earlestown, got one of his feet fast in the wheel. It was carried round until it got jammed between the spokes and the spring, and his screams attracting the notice of the driver, the lurry was stopped and the boy extricated. It was thought his leg was broken and he was put on the lurry and taken home, but on an eaamination being made by Dr. Mouncey, it was found that the leg was badly twisted, and that the lad had marvel- lously escaped very serious injury. He attended to the injuries but the lad is still unable to walk. EARLESTOWN WESLEY GUILD.

The weekly meeting of this Guild was held in the lecture hall of the Wesleyan Chapel, Earlestown,on Wednesday,when there was a good number of mem- bers. The evening's programme was a paper by the Rev. J. Bartley, entitled "A critique on Donovan," Edna Lyal's book. Mr. J H. Profit presided. Mr. Bartley's paper was cleverly written, and in the course of his exposition, he literally pulled ta•ts book to pieces, dicclosing its weakness, and discon- nected plot, alleging that it was badly designed, whilst its main features were really matters of im- possibility. Some slight references were made by Messrs. Pearson, J. Parr, and others.

div.head: FAMILY DISPEITH AT NEWTON._
div.p: FAMILY DISPEITH AT NEWTON._

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, William Edmund Winstanley, No thfleld-square, Leeds, sued his sister, Martha Winstanley, High-st., Newton, for .£l6 18s. Id. for goods supplied. There was also a counterclaim for £5O formoney lent. Mr. Arthur Brovcde represented the plaintiff, and Mr. W. J. Forshaw the defendant. The two partners were formerly in partnership in a plumbing business and the dispute was with reference to certain bills which had to be paid. The case took up consider- able time and numerous items of accounts were ex- amined, and a number of witnesses were called. At the close of the case his Honour held that no doubt the money claimed in the counterclaim was owing, but not by the plaintiff. She could of course sue for it again. He must under the circumstances give judgment for the plaintiff both on the claim and counterclaim.
VIADUCT INSTITUTE (EABLESTOWN) BOWLING CLUB.

The closing match of -t-h-e- season in connection with this club, took place on Saturday on the club green. The two captains, Messrs. Gee and Compton, selected teams, and after a good gatre, the result showed a win for Mr. Gee by 10 points. The follow- ing are the scores : ME. GEE'S TEAM. MR. COM-PTO9 TE.A.X. J. At the conclusion of the match the players and several friends adjourned to the Viaduct Hotel where they partook of a substantial knife and fork tea, provided by Mr. A. Tunstall. After the cloth had been removed, Mr. Joseph Emmett presided over the subsequent proceedings, which were of a social character. Several toasts were propc ed and duly honoured, and songs and recitatio is were con- tributed by the following: Messrs. Huddleston,J. Gibbons, J. Edgar, J. Finch, R. Sherlock, J. Dale, J. and R. Green,J. Allan, J. Gee and R. Smith. During the evening the chairman presented two gold medals, the gift of Mr. A. Tunstall, to Mr. J. Gee and Mr. James Watson for the best club average in tt e Legh Challenge Cup competition during the season. Their averages were : —J. Gee, played five matches, score 104 against 62 by his opponents, average 84. J. Watson played six matches, scored 115, against 101, average 2.33. div.head: SHIP CANAL,
div.p: SHIP CANAL,
ALLEGED SEQUEL TO A SHIP CANAL PICNIC. DEATH OF A LIVERPOOL COTTON BROKER.

The "Liverpool Echo "of Thursday, says :—We re- gret to announce the death of Mr. Edward Melladew,of the firm of Messrs. Melladew and Clarke, cotton brokers, and son of the late Mr. Alderman Melladew. His death isattributed to typhoid fever contracted during a jour- ney up the Manchester Ship Canal with other members oZ the Liverpool Cotton Association, on the occasion of a special trip organised by the Manchester Cotton Asssci- ation on the 21st September last, and to subsequent complications. Two other members of the Cotton As- ,oniation are also suffering from complaints contracted L.ng the same visit of inspection. The death of Mr. Meadew is sincerely regretted bv his fellow brokers, by whom he was hel din the highest esteem. Mr. Melladew ent<ired into the partnership f Mr. Thomas Clarke in in 1866, and the firm has atm) ys held a high position in the market.

div.head: WHOLESALE THEFT OF GROCERIES AT HALTON.
div.p: THE WHOLESALE THEFT OF GROCERIES AT HALTON.

At linutsford Quarter Sessions on Monday, Annie Travis, 51, of Halton, was charged with stealing and receiving 111 b. of butter, 531 b. of bacon, and other goods, the property of John Henry Gamon and another, at Halton, on the 7th August. William Travis (on bail) was charged with receivin.; the goods knowing the.n to be stolen. The woman pleaded guilty. Mr. Yates ap- peared to prosecute, and Mr. E. H. Lloyd defended the ,male prisoner.—The evidence went to show that the pri- eoners were man and wife,and that the woman had been employed by the prosecutors to clean up the shop on Wednesday afternoons. She went on the 7th August, and as she was returning home a pence constable ob- served that her clothing was bulky. He stopped her, and having questioned her he took her to his house, where she was searched by his wife. The bags (pro- duced) were found tied round her waist, and they con- tained a quantity of groceries. A search was afterwards made at the prisoner's house, and quits a stock of goods was found in different parts of the premises. Many of the goods were identified by the prosecutors as their prop-rty,and it was suggested that the husband:knew Lis goods were stolen.—Mr. Lloyd, for the defence, pointed out that when he was charged by the constable the husband said, " I am innocent, I know nothing about them." There could be no doubt that the wife made the bags for the purpose of pilfering. She had been selling groceries to her own son week by week as a re- gular thing. The police charged her son with stealing these things, but after hearing the evidence the magic- I trates discharged him, and sent the woman for trial. They had evidence of the fact that the man had borne an excellent character, and that notwithstanding this charge his employer, who believed in his honesty, was prepared to take him back. They had also the statement of the wife that her husband knew nothing about the gods being stelen.—The jury found the prisoner not guilty and he was discharged.—Mr. Colt Williams, on behalf of the woman, asked the Court to deal mercifully with her, bearing in mind her previous good character. —The Chairman said it was quite clear that she must have been robbing ths firm for some considerable time. It was impossible to account for all those bags and bas- kets, and things in her house without feeling thst toe thefts must have been extended over a very consideratdo time. The bags found upon her showed that there had been a system about it. He thought they were erring en the side of leniency in ordering her to be further im- pri.nned for four months.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICI. Y.P.S.C.E.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICI. Y.P.S.C.E.
AUTUMNAL CONVENTION.

The autumnal convention in connection with the War- rington:and District Young People's Societies of Christian Endeavour was held in the Emmanuel Church,Bold-street Warrington, on Saturday. A conferenos was held in the afternoon and was preceded by a devotional meeting. The Rev. C. Andrews was announced to conduct this meeting, but the Rev. E. T. Reed announced that he had received a letter from that gentleman which stated that in consequence of a somewhat serious illness he would not be able to be present. He said that be had been looking forward to the convention with great delight, and it was with great regret that he was not able to come. Hi, (Mr. Reed) had written to the Rev. J. R. Barnsley of Lymm who had most kindly at the last moment consented to conduct the meeting. The devo- tional meeting was opened with singing, and prayer y Mr. Hutchinson. There were also present besides the Rev. J. R. Barnsley, the Rev. E. T. Reed..the Rev. W. J. Kirklacd, Rev. James Mureell, Mr. Henry Hutchinson, Londoo.Mr. -John Crumblehulme,Bolton,and Mrs. Higge, and Mr. Arthur Mounfield, secretary. The devotional meeting consisted of singing, prayer, and the reading of the scriptures. The Chairman ad- dressing the meeting said that they were met for prayer that afternoon which was a proper thing for them to do. It was' a good thing to begin the meeting that day by first of all seeing the face of their Father and drawing near to Him in supplication and prayer. It was very important that they should get near to God at the be- ginning of their meeting, and in humble confidence, and in faith believing that God would fulfil all His promises to them. Several members of the congregation then en- gaged in prayer.

div.head: CONFERENCE.
div.p: THE CONFERENCE.

After the close of the devotional meeting which oc- cupied half a hour the convention was held, the Rev. E. T. Reed occupying the chair. After opening with a hymn," Come Holy Spirit come," the president's ad- dress was given. The Rev. E. T. REED in his address said that he bad much pleasure en behalf of the officers and members of that church and of the Christian Endeavour Society in giving all present a very hearty welcome to that, the fourth convention of the Warrington and District Association, and of Christian Endeavour Societies. The first 0; these conventions as they were aware was held in Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom in February, 1894, and it was a very successful gathering. Since then, in its wisdom, the Wesleyan Conference had deemed it best to have a separate denominational society, on somewhat similar lines as the Christian Endeavour Movement, but called by the name of the Wesley Guild. While wishing this movement every success and the blessing of God, it was, he thought to be much regretted that the Wesleyan Conference did not see its way to accept the Christian Endeavour Movement in its entirety and to ally them- selves in it for the purpose of Christian co-operation and Christian fellowship. The second convention was held at Newton-le-Willows and it likewise was a most success- ful gathering resulting in the strengthening of the work in that neighbourhood. The third convention waseas they all knew, held in Wycliffe Church in Febru- ary last, and it proved to be a time of blessing and an inspiration to all who were present. With regard to the present convention it was thought by the Executive Committee that it would be most helpful to all the Isocietic3 if the autumnal convention were held in the Iprincipal town in the area covered by the association so that it might give an impetus to the work all over the district. He had wished much to have a convention in his own church. This with the co-operation of his friends the officers of that church, and of their Christian Endeavour Society, had now been brought about, and they bad honoured them with their presence that day. The work in the district would be dealt with that night by the Secretary, Mr. Mouofield, who in the midst of bu less and other cares had devoted a great amount of time to the work of the association. 1 hioughout the Lountry Christian Endeavour Societies continued to in- ease. At the Birmingham convention in June last, there were 2.845 societies reported. The number was now 2,830, an increase of nearly 200 societies during the four summer and holiday months. There would no doubt be great a Ivances during the next four months after the churches he 1• begun their winter campaign. At Bristol next Whitsuntide, the new National Constitu- tion would come into operation and when that was the ca. the movement in the United Kingdom would no doubt go forward even more vigorously and aggres- sively. It was to be regretted that the Church of Eng- land had rot, except in . a few instances, taken up the movement on this side the Atlantic. There was, how- ever, no reason whatever why Evangelical clergymen of the Ettablished Church should not warmly welcome this movement and it was to be hoped that the time was not f r distent when a Christian Endeavour Society would be found in connection with every Evangelical Church whether established or free. The movement was quite inter•demorinational while by its principles it inculcated loyalty to one's own church. About the work through- out the world be would not speak, as Mr. Mursell would, no doubt, bring before them some interesting facts re- sp. ilting his . :nt visit to the Boston Convention, facts which would show the great advance which had been made all over the world, and the ler-ons to be learnt there. An. As to the work of the future,its success and , .ruitfulness dep aded almost entirely upon the spiritual 'Mon of each individual Christian Eodeavourer. ,t was their relation to Christ to-day. Were they relying von Him for salvation ? Were they abiding in Him ? Apart from Him they could do nothing ; but by abiding in Him they could bring forth much fruit. Vario is speake. of experience would bring before them the be3t methods o doing Chris .an work amongst the young and the grown up, and ie connection with the mission field,and he trusted that each Endeavourer there that day would receive a great spiritual and mental stimu' is to renewed earnestness in the work of the Lord ad f. viour Jesus Christ. Mr. HENRY HUTCHINSON, of London, the organising secretary of the children's special service mission, next gave an address upon "Christian Endeavour and the ' children." lie said that it was a great joy to be there that afternoon to have a little fellowship with them in Wr -rington in that blessed work of winning the young ! for Je3tDl, and putting them in e_rness. There was a remarkable contrast in the state of the Christian churches only 30 years ago especially in reference to the young. Mr. Hutchinson proceeded to give an interest- log account of the formation of the Christian Special Service mission. He showed all the difficulties which lay in the way of work among the young at that time— about 30 years ago. He believed that the conversion of children was not only possible but a blessed reality. He had worked in Sunday schools for 37 years, but he thought that the work had failed in one important par- ticular and that was seeking the definite conversion of the children. They had found from experience that the young could clearly and definitely accept the Lord Jesus Cnrist even in tender years, and was so clear as to after favourable comparison with those of older years. It should therefore be the object of the Christian Endea- vour to lead the children individually to Christ. God honoured definiteness of teaching. During the present summer he had held 50 seaside meetings at a large num- ber of watering places, and the results were so clear and definite as to leave no possible room for doubt. Thirty years ago there was much unbelief in reality of conver- sion, but that was all changed at the present time. The great revival in missionary work during the last ten years was in a great measure due to the work among the children for the past twenty years. Some years ago,the church refused to allow the children to take part in the Communion, but now they frequently saw little en- deavourers at the table,and bethought that the Lord had got se' :or every one to do. What he loved about the EnJo.vour was that it got the little ones in harness so soon. He hoped that God would richly encourage them and give them great success in their work. He hoped they would be mightily successful. He hoped they would not be discouraged that the Wesleyans had started a little one of their own. That always hap- pened. When the Salvation Army was so successful,the Church began a Church Army. Emulation was the sin- cerest form of flattery, and no doubt after a tim-, Wesleyans would come back to them, (Applause.)

Mr. Jam; CIiIIMBLEBULME. of Bolton,, then gave an address upon " Christian Endeavour and Evangelistic work.' He said that the subject be had to speak upon was the most important subject that could engage the attention of any convention in the Christian community, He wished that afternoon to give a few words of en- couragement to those who were engaged in the Christian Endeavour work. The work of the Lord was not con- fined to the mighty. He believed in personal influence and contact. He nimself was brought into the church by that means. Mr. Crumblehulme gave a number of interesting anecdotes to illustrate his address.

Mrs. Moos, president of the Oldham and District Association, then gave an addresa upon "Christian En- deavour and foreign missions. She said that she intended to re-christen her paper. She objected to the word foreign. She was going to speak about Christian En- deavour in other lands. Christian Endeavour was catholic and world wide. The time was not far distant in the history of the world when the English were foreigners. It was not long ago when people sent mis- 'sione over here to convert the English, and now the latter turned round and called the rest of the world foreign. She believed that this distinction was the curse of the times. They did not hear people talking of trade as tey talked shout miss,ons.They never heard of any man- ; uf uturere refusing any opening for trade in other lands, because he was ever ready to develop his trade. He did not wait until th• English people had enough and plenty of clothes or luxuries before supplying the people of other lands. If the service of the god mammon were progressive, and the service for the Man Christ Jesus was insular and unprogressive, so much the worse for Christianity. Let them all forget the distinctions of time and race. Mrs. Higgs then proceeded to give an account of the work in Mad agascar, the South Sea Islands, India, China and Africa. She thought that they in England ought to dowle their ranks. 'itch Christian Endeavour Society ought to endeavour to link them. selves with some foreign mission, and correspond with them and so by standing behind them, help them. She hoped that they would go forward in the strength of Christ Jesus.
A "free parliament" was then held at which various

div.head: EVENING MEE LING.
div.p: EVENING MEE LING.
There was a good attendance in the evening, when the chair was occupied by the Rey. W. H. Towers, president 61f the Manchester and District Union. After singing aid prayer, _ _

The Rev. JAMES MIIRSELL gave an address upon " American Christian Endeavour as seen at Boston, 1895." He said that to talk abmt Boston in 1395 in 25 minutes or half-an-hour seemed almost impossible there was so much to say, there were so many points of inter- est that 0143 was almost inclined to sit in one's chair dis- tracted considering how to make a speech upon it. It called to one's mind that picture of the great Christian Eadeavour throng of all creeds of youths and maidens, the very Hower of America.and not lacking either in the ' flower of other countries besides America, all of them , with the same object. He had a better right than many of them in giving an account of it, as he went there as a [ private individual. When he arrived at Boston, he ' found the city in a great state of excitement owing to the Convention. The greatest buildings vitro magnific- ently decorated, and even at a public-house they were selling Christian Endeavour punch. (Laughter.) A policeman, however, soon put a stop to the sale of this. At night the buildings were lit up with electric light with Christian Endeavour devices,and in the park or gardens, tie beds were laid out in Christian Endeavour style,with even attempts at portraiture of prominent endeavourers, by order of the C3rporation. They had a most magni- licent reception. The newspapers also gave the Conven- tion the notice it deserved. There were columns of verbatim reports of it, and there were also interviews with prominent men in connection with it. A large portion of the paper was also taken up with portraits and scenes of the Convention, and in this respect, the English papers were far behind those of America. The meetings were magnificent assemblages, and it was a grand and solemn sight to see the enormous number present at them. They met in two tents, and an idea of the number present might be had when he stated that there were 56,030 delegates alone. The Americans were not afraid of showing their colours and he saw the colours of the Endeavour everywhere. They ought never to be ashamed of being Christians. They wanted men who could take their side in the battle of life. The kindness with which they were received by Dr. Clarke would be impossible to describe. They were received by him in the kindliest manner, and he would never forget the time spent with him. In conclusion he said that that Convention was a memorable one,and one which he would always remember, and he also hoped that the Christian Endeavour in Warrington district would prosper. (Applause.) Mr. ARTHER MOUNFIELD, the hon. secretary of the district, said that he was quite sure that it must have been a singular pleasure to have listened to Mr. Mursell [ that night when he was talking about some of the won- derful possibilities of the Christian Endeavour. If the occasion had been a secular one, it would have been remarkable, but when they remembered that Christian Endeavour was for out and out consecration to Jesus Christ, they could not describe their feelings towards it. He was inclined to wish that there were another voice there that night as eloquent and as strong as Mr. Mursell, to apply the message with regard to the War- rington district. Personally, he lthe speaker) felt deeply indebted to him, as he had shown the possibilities of the Christian Endeavour. (Hear, hear.) But while Mr. acumen talked about his 60,000, he would talk about his 630. With regard to his report, he might say that just before the meeting began, he had received a note from their Wesleyan friends withdrawing from their associa- tion on the ground that they were forming a Wesley Guild. At the commencement of the year there were in the district eleven societies and now there were 14, with a prospect of adding another at their next executive meeting. (Applause.) There were 397 members, 169 associates and 54 honarary members, making a total membership of 620. It was even more encouraging that they had eight junior societies against five that time last year, with a membership of 370 members. They had not yet reached the ideal, nor should they until they had a junior branch connected with each society. They all believed in what they were doing; they believed that in this fellowship amongst themselves they were finding a real blessing. The basis of their union was loyalty to Christ; their grandest ideal was to do whatever Jesus Christ would have them do. He hoped that the junior branches would increase, for it was a definite part of the association's aim to look after the children; and then the duties they had to perform would every year be done better and would bear more fruit. Mr. H. H. HOPE. %ice president of the Liverpool and District Union, next addressed the meeting on Christian Endeavour and good citizenship. He said man's life was not expressed in what he said, but in what he did, or rather in what he was. The badge of good citizen- ship was the white flower of a blameless life. How could a man be a good citizen if he lived an impure Every thought and every act not only debased himself , but broke down the structure of civic law and the ' cohesive principles which bound a community together. A good citizen was one who respected and obeyed the Is vs of his country; good government demanded due submission 10 the powers that be. He should render unto Cseiar the things that were Cmiar's and to God the things that were God's. Every citizen should conduct himself so as to be a pattern of goodness to his neigh- bours, and this was what Christian Endeavourers were trying to bring about. If in the past the Christian Church had done her duty—he was not finding fault now —the world would not to-day be facing the drink prob- lem. No man nor woman living, he dared say, could truthfully declare that the drink curse had never touched their lives through relative or friend. Had good citizen- [ ship vindicated itself, would there be existing to-day 1 some of the beastly unhealthy dwellings which the poor lived in, and which spread debility and vice around them all ? Was it good citizenship to damn the evil woman and indemnify the evil man ? Why should they not be equally amenable V& the law ? Until both men and women were equal in the eyes of the law, there would always exist a barrier across the path of the Christian Endeavourers, and they would do well to try to remove it. The children of a drunken father should to taken away from him; he should not , be allowed to debase them as he had debased himself. Parents had a national responsibility as well as an indi- vidual responsibility, and the Legislature ought not to look upon the manufacture of children into criminals without interfering. Christian citizenship, which the Endeavour movement aimed at developing, entered a loud protest to everything which made its way towards evil, and if the members acted up to their principles and were zealous, that protest would soon have its de- sired effect.

The CHAIRMAN afterwards gave an address on " The Holy Spirit in our Works." He appealed to his fellow Christian Endeavourers to place their souls in such a focus that they might be endowed with power through the Divine Spirit. It was through the influence of the Holy Spirit that the movement had accomplished what it had, and it would go on accomplishing good things in spite of all that might be said or done against it, if only it possessed the influence of the Holy Spirit. If the Christian Christ and young Endeavourers would only be obedient to the Holy Spirit, this world would soon be in a better state ; and if they yielded themselves fully to the working ot the Divine haly power that was within them, they would then find that God was using them in their sphere—quietly, but nevertheless effectively—for the regeneration of this lost world.
A consecration meeting subsequently took place, con. ducted by the Rev. W. H. Towers, and after other de- votions the Convention was brought to a termination by the singing of the Mizpah Benediction.
