At the League Hall in;:t7ng on Sunday last Mr. J. C. Dalton delivered a leture on tee above subject. In course of his address Mr. Halton said that the "romance of Maria Monk" originally appeared in a New York paper called the "Protestant Vindicator," as far back as the year 1835, just sixty years ago, and notwithstanding the fact, that a complete re- futation of the calumnies, appeared at the time,and that the Protestant Press in Montreal, 'where these fearful acts were said to have occurred, stated in the most emphatic way, ti.at the allegation of Maria Monk against the " Venerable Catholic Bishop the devoted Catholic clergy and the self sacrificing ' Nuns, was a foul and wicked calumny from beginn- ing to end." Mr. Dalton concluded by saying that a different spirit was now evident among respect- able protestant people. They no longer regarded Catholics as monsters of iniquity. Father Damien by his noble sacrifice in leper-island had open4d the eyes of the Protestant people regarding the mcrality of the Catholic priesthood and as evidence to point, he said that when a Preteqtant gentleman like Mr. James Hill of Minnesota built a grand col- lege costing him £lOO,OOO as a mark or esteem for a Catholic prelate, they could afford to treat with scorn and contempt such calumnious romances as Maria Monk. Mr. Mullins also addressed the meet- ing, and several men took the total abstinence pledge. The attendance at holy communion was very large and satisfactory.
EXTRAORDINARY INCIDENT AT

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.
HEROIC CONDUCT OF A RUNCORN
PUBLICAN.

Two children of Mr. F. Rutter, of Windmill-st., Runcorn, narrowly escaped suffocation on Thurs- day afternoon. It appears that the house of their grandparents is right, opposite, and this was being fumigated by an officer of the Runcorn Urban Council. The children gained access to the house un- noticed, and the officer not perceiving their pre- sence, locked them in on completing his work. Fortunately the cries of the children were heard by some neighbours, and they raised an alarm. Mr. W. Powell, landlord of the Bull's Head, Halton- road, gained access to the house by means of a ladder which enabled him to get through a bed- room window. He found the two chil- dren in a state of complete exhaustion and succeeded in rescuing them from their perilcus position. Mr. Powell took the pre- caution of wrapping a curtain over his face, but notwithstanding this he was almost overcome with the fumes. The desinfectants had been placed in the kitchen, and it is supposed that the children whose ages ranged from four to six years, had opened the kitchen door in their endeavours to get out of the house, and thus caused the fumes to ex- tend throughout the house. Mr. Powell is to be congratulated on hie heroic deed, especially as we understand that it is not the first occasion on which he has been instrumental in saving life.

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

HALTON-ROAD MISS/ON Cannel:L-0n Thursday week, the harvest thanksgiving services were commenced. The church was beautifully decorated. The preacher was the vicar, the Rev. G. D. Wray. On Sunday afrernoon, the Vicar conducted a children a service, and in the evening, Mr. Dew preached. A collection was taken at each service. The fruit was, subsequently, distributed amongst the poor in the neighbourhood. GIRLS' SCROOL.—The annual concert and distribution of prizes, took place on Friday. The winners received their prizes from the hand of Mrs. Carruthers, who delivered an appropriate speech. There was a large audience, and the following programme was gone through in a manner which reflects great credit on those responsible for the training of the children :—Opening chorus, "Canadian Boat Song"; recitation, "An Address," Maude Ashley; recitation, "Which," Ethel Saunders; dumb-bell drill; song (Infants), "The Mouse "' recitation," The Village Choir," Ada Murphy ; fan ; recitation, "Grandma," Mabel Hancock ; prose recitation," The husband who minded the house," Selina Bazley ; tambourine drill ' • chorus, " The days of long ago" ; musical medley, "The Tonic Sol-fa class." Miss Edwards and Miss Moores acted as accompanists. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS.—On Sunday the annual sermons on behalf of foreign missions were preached in the Wesleyan Church, in the morning by the Bev. T. Brackenbury, and in the evening by the Rev. C. de P. Gliddon. The choir sang the anthems "The Lord is loving," and "King of Kings." In the former Mr. T. Barrow sang the bass solo, and Mr, H. Rowe the tenor ; in the latter the tenor solo was rendered by Mr. A. Saunders. Mr. Sutton played the organ. There were good congregations, and a collection was taken at each service.

WasLETAN CIIIIRCW—On Thursday week a large num- ber of young people and those interested in their wel- fare gathered together in the schoolroom to discuss the question of establishing a branch of the "Wesley Guild." Mr. Lea presided,and the Rev. C.de P. Gliddon explained the objects and working of the " Guild." There wss a long discussion, and it was decided that a branch should bestarted at once.

div.head: UNITED lIETHODIT3T FREE CHURCHES
div.p: UNITED lIETHODIT3T FREE CHURCHES
CONFERENCE AT FRODSHAM.

The autumnal session of the United Methodist Free Churches in the Liverpool and North Wales district was held in the Methodist Free Church, Frodsham, on Thurs- day. The Rev. J. Truscott (Crewe) occupied the chair, and he was supported by the Rev. Charles Pre (secre- tary), Mr. Thomas Linton (financial secretary), Mr. R. J. Pratt (treasurer), Rev. W. Downing (temperance secretary), and Mr. J. Hoult (temperance treasurer). Other delegates present were Rev. John Naylor (Liver- pool Central), Rev. J. Lathorn and Mr. W. Shallcross (Liverpool north),Rev. S. W. Hopkins (Liverpool south), Rev. W. H. C. Harris and Mr. T. Oakes (Burslern), Mr. J. T. Worthington (Crewe), Rev. R. Percival (Frod- sham), Rev. J. E. Portman (Nantwich), Rev. G. A. Ward and Mr. Ralph Downing (Newcastle-under-Lyme) Rev. J. Taylor and Mr. Jones (Northwieh), Rev. J. Stafford (Runcorn), Rev. Mr. Smith (St. Helens and Prescott), Rev. W. H. Beeken (Winsford and Sandbach), Rev. E. Watmough (supernumerary.) The requested division of the Runcorn and Widnes churches was taken into consideration. The deputation appointed to consider the subjecz reported that they had not been able to recommend the division but had advised the division of ministerial services, and also that the Widnes Church might profitably engage the services of a student occasionally. A hope was expressed that this recommendation would meet the difficulty of the Widnes Church.

Mr. T. Linton, J.P., gave a statement of circuit con- tributions to the various connexional funds. He called attention to the fact that while the mission income of the district had increased, the grant for the mission fund had decreased since 1887 by £403. A committee consisting of the following was appointed for the examination of candidates for the ministry : Revs. J. Taylor, W. Beeken, W. H. C. Harris, atd C. W. Hopkins, Meagre. T Snape, J.P., C.C., R. J. Lloyd, J. R. Pratt, and T. Oakes. It was decided that November 24 should be observed as temperance Sunday throughout the district, snd the all preachers and teachers on that day be requested to enforce temperance principles. They also urged the hold- ing of circuit temperance gatherings preceding and fol- lowing temperance Sunday. With regard to the education question it was resolved that the meeting protested against the proposals to increase the grant of public money to schools under exclusively denominational management. The meeting further declared the conviction that the great educational grievar.ces of Nonconformists could never thus be met, and that the best educational results could never be obtained until there was a general system of School Boards acting In areas of sufficient size to secure justice and efficiency. . _
A pudic nieeting was held in the evening when a number of addresses were delivered.

div.head: PARISH COUNCIL MEETING AT WESTON.
div.p: PARISH COUNCIL MEETING AT WESTON.

The Rev. Canon Wood presided at the meeting of the Weston Parish Council on Friday evening. There were also present, Messrs. T. T. Sill, J. Tudor, L. Rosenberg, J. Ball. D. Barratt, R. R. Clarke, S. Savage, J. Sweet- man, J. Vose, J. Moore, and J., Collier (clerk.)—The Clerk reported that with regard to the footpath in Mr. Thomas Griffith's field, which was considered danger- ous, he had written to Mr. Evans,drawing his attention to the subject, and received a reply asking for a plan. The Clerk further remarked that he had forwarded a plan, and stated that the names of the owners and occu- piers il would receive attention.—Mr. Basnett said from his own ehehhaedlionvbetd t receivedhe suh subject pie r s of informationthe on adjoiningth the subject, la nd* observations the supply of water had been very favour- able since their last meeting. The house on the highest point had a plentiful supply except on e Saturday when the force was somewhat less.— The Clerk read a circular from the Librarian of the Run- corn Free Library showing that the subscription for outsiders, for use of the lending department, had been reduced from 59. to is. per annum.—The Chairman said the Library Committee asked the people residing in Flal ton. Weston and Clifton to share the benefits provided by the Library, at a nominal charge. Considering that it was part of their powers as a Council to form such an institution, they ought to be grateful to them for afford- ing the advaatages without any charge upon the district. —Mr. Sill moved that they express their indebtedness to the Runcorn Library Committee for their kindness, and that the Council bring the matter before the attention of the residents of the township.—Mr. Rosenberg seconded the motion, which was unanimously carried.—The Clerk read a letter received from the Rev. W. H. Stable+ ask- I ing the Council to agree as to the amount to be paid for lighting. warming and cleaning the room in which their meetings were held.—Mr. Rosenberg moved, and Mr. Moore seconded, and it was unanimously resolved that the sum of £1 per annum bepaid to the managers for all meetings to be held in connection with the Council.— Mr. Rosenberg drew attention to the ashpit question, saving nothing satisfactory had -been arranged. De vri,thed a committee to be appointed, to have the power to invite two or three farmers in the township to con- sider the best means of dealing with the nightsoil, and then to recommend their decision to the Council.—Mr. ratlhDeyistrhiact viCneousnac id Council, hut Sill seconded the proposition.—Mr. Vose said the ques- tionw without ohuatd beenany before the resußltu, beneficial owners or tenants must empty the ashpits, or pro- ceedings would he taken against them. Farmers would only take it as it suited their convenience. The D.strict Council had failed to do their duty in the matter Mr. Moore moved an amendment that the committee should consist of four members of the Council and the two district councillors.—Mr. Savage seconded this.— After some further discussion the amendment was lost by eight to two votes.—lt was moved by Mr. Sill, seconded Mr. Clarke and unanimously decided, that a committee consistine• of five of the members of the Council he appointed to consider the question of empty- ing the ashpita in the district, devise a scheme, and place it bef?re the next meeting of the Council. It was also determined that the committee should consist of Mess. Vose, ?doore,Rosenberg,Tudor, and Sill.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Having been urgently requested by many of my f fiends and ratepayers to Nola offer myself as a candidate to repre- sent this ward in the Town Connell, I have decided to comply wit h their wishes. If you elect me as your representative I shall do my utmost to serve you faithfully, and to further the interests of the town. For your confidence in the past accept my thanks. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen. Yours truly. S. J. BEAMAN. 123, Bewsey-road, Warrington, October 15, 1895.

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. UNICIPAL ELECTION, NOVEMBER Mr, IVI 1895. TO THE ELECTORS OF ST. JOHN'S WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Having been invited by a large and influential number of the Electors of this Ward, to offer myself as a Candidate for the va-tancy which occurs on the let November, I do so feeling that I have the confidence and good wishes of the majority of the electors. I am in favour of making prevision for, and encouraging the laying down and constructing of Tramways through our principal streets, as I am of opinion that this would tend to Improve the general trade of our town. If this were brought abont it would have the effect of increasing the number of re- sidents and would give employment to all claves of trades interested in building and constructive operations. It will be my err leavour,as far as lam able to bring about the widening of the various streets, so long under considera tion, as early as possible. I believe that the sooner this improvement is carried out, the less expensive it will be. I am also in favour of all work being, when practicable, carried out by local workmen, and full trade prices being paid for the same. I shall at all times do what I can to assist manufacturers and traders to develope their business so that we may have a greater number of works in our midst and, then fore, be in a position to give more employment to all classes of work- people. I am of opinion that the Warrington Town Council has not given that encouragement to local industries which It is in its power to give. The Sanitary condition of our town is very much im- proved but leaves very much to be desired, and lam of opinion that tho amount of sickness that has been prevalent, in this Ward in particnlar, is caused by the foul vapours that from time to time emanate from our sewe.h. I shall endea- vour to get some remedy put into practical operation that will remove all these ohjectionable vapours. If you do me the honour to elect melt will be my earnest endeavour to give special attention to everything relating to the interests of this Borough. lam, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servant, WILLIAM FURNESS, Haydock Street, Warrington. October 11th, 1895.

The information contained in this book ought to be known by every married woman, and it will not harm the unmarriep to read. The book is conveniently divided into 12 chapters The first chapter treats of the changes at puberty, or when a girl becomes a woman. The second chapter treats of marriage from a doctor's standpoint ; points out the best age for marriage, and who should have children and who not, and furnishes useful information that one can ordinarily get only from an intelligent doctor. The third chapter treats of the marriage of blood relations; and condemns such marriages as a rule. Chapter four treats of the signs of pregnancy. The fifth chapter tells how a woman should live during the pregnant state. Tne sixth chapter treats f mishaps and how to avoid them. The seventh chapter treats of materna I impressions and shows that birthmarks are not due to longings on the part of the mother, but rather to her poor health. The eighth chapter teaches how to have easy confinements. Certain people believe that women should bring forth in pain and trouble, but the hygienic physician says that confinements can be made comparatively easy If certain rules are obeyed ; these rules are given. The ninth chapter treats of the proper management of confinement until the baby is born. The tenth chapter tells how to treat he mother till she is up and about again. The eleventh chapter treats of sterility ; gives the main causes of it, how these may be overcome and children result. The last chapter treats of the "change," a most important article for all women over forty. The book is full of useful information and no book is written which goes BO thoroughly into matters relating to married women. Some may think too much is told ; such can scarcely be the case, for knowledge is power and the means of attaining happiness. T e book can be ha 1 coin Dr. T. SHIP CANAL. --- LAST ;WEEK'S TRAFFIC ON THE CANAL. During the week ending Friday, October 11, 142 sea- going cargo vessels, with an aggregate net registered tonnage of 40,571 tons, arrived at and sailed from the port of Manchester, which includes all parts of the Ship Canal. The number of arrivals and departures during the preceding week was 115, and the net tonnage 32,934, showing an increase last week of 27 ships and 7,537 tons. This was almost exclusively in the coastwise traffic, which increased by 33 ships and 7,422 tons, whilst vessels engaged in the foreign trade were fewer by six, although their net tonnage was slightly greater. Amongst the full cargoes entered inwards were eight of china clay, five of pig-iron, four of wood-pulp, two of timber, and one each of setts, slate, limestone, waste salt, bog ore, steel girders, logwood, green fruit, and currants. The full cargoes exported included six of salt, three of coal, and three of pitch.

A,VEEKLY CHAT.—SUBJECT "THE PANTHEON." ! 4' The successful establishment of any of the large ware- houses of Manchester is always of interest to the citizens. One , of the most brilliant examples of the value of perseverance, en- terorise, and tact, is the now busy hive of industry se well . known as The Pantheon, which occupies such a prominent position in Gaythorn, near the Central Station, Manchester. . The building is a massive pile of modern design, 150 feet long, six storeys high, with showroom accommodation, cover- t ing an area of over one million square feet. The plate glass windows are each 12 feet square, each square if bro'i en cost- , lug £3O to replace. Ten of these immense show windows form a portion of the frontage. This will give a taiut idea of" The Pantheon "in outward appearance, but ah I—here pen fails altogether in attempting to do justi le to anything like an adequate description of the interior. " The Pantheon" was speaialfy built to give the largest and most convenient ' floor space for showroomss and cost £28,000, the floors speci- ally constructed to carry enormous weight. To-day it stands : as one of the smartest furnishing houses in England, contain- ing by far the largest ...nd most comprehensive stock of any : two houses in, this large city. From basement to roof, from floor to ceiling, 'The Pantheon "is filed to overflowing with thousands Of well bought, carefully selected bargains, to at- tempt description of which would be as futile as Liverpool . attempting to crush THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. The destinies of" The Pantheon" are cmtrolled and pre- sided over by its sole absolute proprietor, Mr. W. H.
